kikuyu: Agikuyũ moi kũhitha ndia, matiũ kuhitha ũhoro
translation: The Kikuyu know how to conceal their quiver, but do not know how to conceal their secrets.
explanation: The Kikuyu, though very clever in concealing their arms, cannot keep secrets from the members of their tribe.

translation: Two guests (at the same time) have no welcome.
Two guests love a different song.
explanation: When you receive two visitors at the same time, you cannot treat them in the same manner, because they have different tastes.
englishEquivalent: Every man has his hobby horse.

translation: He is a man that looks after money as ‘njũ’ looks after locusts.
explanation: ‘Njũũ’ is a bird which accompanies migrating locusts to feed on them.
englishEquivalent: Much wants more.

kikuyu: Aka eri ni nyũngũ igĩrĩ cia ũrogi
translation: Two wives are two pots full of poison.
explanation: The more women you have in your house, the more troubles you must expect.
englishEquivalent: Women’s jars breed men’s wars.

kikuyu: Aka matĩrĩ cia ndiiro no cia nyiniko
translation: Women have no upright words, but only crooked ones.
explanation: The Kikuyu use the proverb to say that women keep no secrets and seldom tell the truth.
englishEquivalent: Women conceal all that they know not.

translation: Wives and oxen have no friends.
explanation: There are things which are not to be given to friends. A woman is to be from her house three times: when she is christened, married, and buried.

translation: Men are equal when they are going and walking.
explanation: One can notice a difference between man and man when they, ‘exempli gratia’, are commanding or working, but not on the road where they look quite the same.

kikuyu: Andũ matari ndundu mahũragwo na njũgũma ũmwe
translation: People who have no secret agreement are beaten by a single club.
explanation: A group of men not bound by a secret will be easily beaten by a single man.
englishEquivalent: Lack of union spells weakness.

translation: Men do not know liberality.
englishEquivalent: One does not give without hope of return.

translation: Men do not know hard firewood, but only lops.
englishEquivalent: People put aside hard tasks and devote themselves only to easy ones.

translation: Live men do not lack work.
englishEquivalent: Life would be too smooth if it had no rubs in it.

translation: He who seeks his goat with the man who ate it, is certain not to find it.
englishEquivalent: Do not look for stolen goods in the robber's house.

translation: Men have got quills.
explanation: Do not annoy others because they will respond by hurting.
englishEquivalent: Do evil and look for like.

translation: Necessities never end.
englishEquivalent: He that will have no trouble in this world must not be born in it.

translation: The elders drink afterwards (i.e.
explanation: after the others).
englishEquivalent: Elderly people are not in such a hurry as young ones.

translation: The food found Wacũ in the field.
explanation: The proverb originates in the legend of Wacũ, the most despised amongst the wives of a rich man who never

translation: The property of a helpless man must not be divided before his death.
englishEquivalent: The reason is that he is unable to get anything more than he already possesses.

kikuyu: Cia mūciĩ irĩ gacūgūma gacio gatathukagio ni mūthuri
translation: ūngĩ tīga mweneguo Home affairs have their staff, which cannot be brandished by anyone but the head of the house.
explanation: The proverb means either that private matters must not be spoken of to strangers or that in each house there must be only one in authority.

translation: Home affairs must not go into the open.
englishEquivalent: Do not wash dirty linen in public

translation: Home affairs cannot be told in public.
englishEquivalent: Do not wash dirty linen in public

translation: The widow's sons have no tears.
explanation: It means that they have been accustomed to suffer very early.

translation: Birds agree when flying down, but do not agree when flying up.
Bought things do not fill the granary.
englishEquivalent: Do not hope to become rich without cultivating your fields.

translation: When there is shortage of figs, birds eat the fruits of the ‘mugumo’.
explanation: The tree called ‘mugumo’ by the natives bears little fruits that are not eaten by birds when there is plenty of other food.
englishEquivalent: If thou hast not a capon, feed on an onion.

translation: The buying of a wife begins from a little thing.
englishEquivalent: Great events have small beginnings.

translation: Goats fall that take hold of lichens.
explanation: Lichens are not strong enough to prevent a goat from falling. The proverb means that unsatisfactory excuses are insufficient defence.

kikuyu: Cionje ikũmi irũgĩtĩwo ni ũmwe ũri na hinya
translation: Ten helpless people were surpassed by a single strong person.
explanation: One strong person is better than ten helpless ones.
englishEquivalent: One grain of pepper is worth a cartload of hail.

translation: A long lawsuit breeds poverty.
englishEquivalent: Fools and obstinate men make lawyers rich.

kikuyu: Cira mūnene ni wa ūthoni ūgikua
translation: The breaking-up of a betrothal is no small matter.
explanation: Marrying a girl means giving a large number of goats or cattle to her family. Starting from the day of the betrothal the price is paid gradually. Evidently it is no simple matter if the would-be husband breaks his contract and demands the return of the marriage price.

translation: The lawsuit of a fool keeps the court (sitting) all day.
englishEquivalent: The lawsuit of a fool never comes to an end.

translation: Home affairs are not to be carried on in the public square.
englishEquivalent: Do not wash dirty linen in public.

translation: Every case begins from the stomach.
explanation: The Kikuyu have an ox or a goat killed, roasted and distributed to judges at the beginning of every case. Familiarly they use the proverb to say that one of the most important jobs of life is to provide something to eat.
englishEquivalent: An empty belly hears nobody.

translation: We speak by proverbs: he who is intelligent will understand .
englishEquivalent: Intelligenti pauca.

translation: Clear out of the ‘thakirio’.
explanation: ‘Thakirio’ is the place in the Kikuyu hut where the wife stays when distributing the food to the family.
englishEquivalent: Mind your own business.

translation: He who spends his time adorning himself knows he is going to a dance.
englishEquivalent: There is a reason for everything.

translation: He who adorns himself knows to what sort of dance he is going.
englishEquivalent: There is a reason for everything.

translation: The fool takes many people with him.
explanation: It is said of people who, when invited to a feast, instead of going alone, take many others with them.
englishEquivalent: A fool cannot bear his own company.

kikuyu: Garũria mbeũ ti ya kĩnya kimwe
translation: Change seeds taking them from different calabashes.
englishEquivalent: It is good to introduce new blood.

kikuyu: Gatami kari mondo yene gatingikũratira nguo
translation: The piece of cloth that is in another's bag does not patch your garment.
A little, contemptible path is sometimes the one that leads you to the highway.
englishEquivalent: Little strokes fell great oaks.

kikuyu: Gatitũ ka mũimwo ni irĩ noko kari miti
translation: The forest of an unpleasant (ill-liked) person is the one that has trees.
explanation: The proverb means that evil-doers often do prosper.

translation: The grove of the heart is not laid open.
Nobody cries that has not been pinched.
englishEquivalent: No smoke without fire.

translation: Darkness causes to dance even him who cannot.
englishEquivalent: All cats are the same in colour at night.

translation: A secret agreement enabled people to kill Watatua.
explanation: Watatua was a powerful Chief, invincible in open combat, who was killed at night by a few men.
englishEquivalent: Secret union means strength.

translation: A market can be spoilt by one woman.
englishEquivalent: One cloud is enough to eclipse the sun.

translation: Every feast has its guest of honour.
One appointment is eaten by another.
englishEquivalent: Today kills yesterday.

translation: That of circumcision is a hard appointment.
explanation: The Kikuyu circumcision is a civil and religious rite by which the adolescent is admitted into the public life of the tribe and becomes a man in the full possession of his rights. The ceremony is physically painful, but the candidate is expected to face the operation without wincing.
englishEquivalent: There are no gains without pains.

translation: To wait is not to tremble.
englishEquivalent: Men's actions are not to be judged at first sight.

kikuyu: Gicegũ kia andũ aingi ti kiega
translation: The 'gicegũ' of many men is not good.
A piece of land is not a little thing.
explanation: The proverb means that however small the field you possess, it has its importance if you work it. A little house well filled, a little land well tilled, a little wife well willed are great riches.

kikuyu: Gĩkaro kimwe kĩri ngee kana ndaa
translation: By staying always in the same place one gets lice.
explanation: The world is a great book, of which they that never stir from home read only one page.

translation: The only thing good, though old, is the ‘mũratina’.
explanation: ‘Mũratina’ is the fruit of the hot-dog tree (Kigelia Etiopica) used by the natives to cause fermentation of sugar-cane beer. It is believed that the older the fruit, the greater is its fermenting power. The proverb means that there are only few things that improve with age.

translation: You cannot (do not) make an appointment with death.
The land enriches not people who clear it, but people who come (when it is already cleared).
englishEquivalent: One beats the bush, and another catches the bird.

translation: Lying is the thief's stronghold.
Beggars have no worries.
englishEquivalent: Poverty needs no granary.

translation: The chest contains a beehive full of pride.
explanation: The proverb means that proud people have always in store lots of reasons justifying their wickedness.

translation: Talking something over is better than leaving it pending.
englishEquivalent: Never leave that till tomorrow which you can do today.

kikuyu: Gitiiro kia mũka wene gitikagio athii
translation: The song of a stranger-woman is answered after she has gone.
explanation: The proverb is metaphorically used to mean that foreigners, especially women, are not to be trusted too much.
englishEquivalent: Eat a peck of salt with a man before you trust him.

translation: It is bad to stay at home.
englishEquivalent: He that stays in the valley shall never get over the hill.

translation: He who does not know, knows after being told.
englishEquivalent: A man forewarned is forearmed.

translation: He who does not know the road delays also one that knows it.
englishEquivalent: Who goes with a fool becomes a fool.

translation: The rich man cannot be prevented from cultivating the 'iganjo' he wants.
explanation: 'Iganjo' is the place upon which a hut had been built. Since the flocks live in the owner's hut, the floor of the hut becomes fertilized. The proverb refers to the fact that if a rich man has left a piece of his land to a poor man on which to build his hut, very often he wants it back as soon as the soil under the hut has been enriched by the droppings of the animals.
englishEquivalent: Might is right.

translation: Rich people sometimes eat bad food.
englishEquivalent: All is not gold that glitters.

translation: Travelling is learning.
englishEquivalent: The world is a great book, of which they that never stir read only one page.

translation: To be slim does not mean having been pared.
englishEquivalent: Do not scorn little things.

translation: The woman who gives birth to a child is like the banana tree that breaks under the weight of its fruit.
englishEquivalent: Maternity means pain to the mother.

kikuyu: Gūciara ūru ti kwenda kwa mwene
translation: It is not the mother’s will to have a bad offspring.
People slander somebody even if they do not despise him.
Riches and poverty do not leave each other.
To keep one’s tongue is worthy of praise.
englishEquivalent: Silence is golden.

translation: Not to talk is to hate.
englishEquivalent: One keeps silence with people one does not like.

translation: Indulgence breeds regret.

kikuyu: Gūkūra ni kūru: ngathī ūrīrī ngicayaga
translation: It is bad to get old, for one goes to bed grumbling.
englishEquivalent: Old sacks want much patching.

translation: The fact that you have gone near the battle-field does not mean that you fought.
Thieves conceal themselves in the night not in the day.
englishEquivalent: The night is a cloak for sinners.

translation: To get the warmth of fire one must stir the embers.
englishEquivalent: No gains without pains.

translation: The fear (of toil) keeps your house poor.
englishEquivalent: Idleness is the key of beggary.

translation: If you help yourself you will be helped.
englishEquivalent: God helps those who help themselves.

kikuyu: Gūtema na kanua ti gūtema na rūhiū
translation: Cutting by the tongue is different from cutting by the knife.
explanation: Slander is not mortal stabbing.
englishEquivalent: Hard words break no bones.

translation: A man changing his abode is like a woman marrying.
explanation: As a woman, on marrying, adopts the customs of the family she enters, so a man going to live in a strange country, must accept its customs.
englishEquivalent: When in Rome do as Rome does.

kikuyu: Gūthekererwo ni andũ ti kūririrwo ni hiti
translation: To be laughed at by men is not to be wept by hyenas.
englishEquivalent: Better to be laughed at than to die.

translation: To be laughed at is not to be pitied.
explanation: One starting any enterprise ought not to fear what others say of him.
englishEquivalent: Do well and dread no shame.

translation: If anybody makes you laugh, it is not always because he loves you.
englishEquivalent: Eat a peck of salt with a man before you trust him.

translation: Some hope for rain even though they have not prepared their fields.
englishEquivalent: He who hopes for favours should have prepared himself to profit by them.

translation: To go does not prevent a man from returning.
englishEquivalent: Never give up.

translation: Travelling teaches men their way.
Travelling is seeing.
englishEquivalent: Travel broadens the mind.

translation: Having rain clouds is not the same as having rain.
englishEquivalent: Don't cry herrings till they are in the net.

translation: Virtue is better than riches.
englishEquivalent: Virtue is the only true nobility.

translation: Virtue is power.
explanation: Virtue makes men on the earth famous, in their graves illustrious, in the heavens immortal.

kikuyu: Gũthũra ng'ombe ni gũthũra kamũkwa kayo
translation: To despise the ox means to despise also a strip of hide from it.
englishEquivalent: One cannot scorn great things without scorning little ones related to them.

translation: One favours him from whom one has in the past received a gift.
englishEquivalent: One good turn deserves another.

translation: A man is (sometimes) scorned who will be loved (later on).
englishEquivalent: Judge not of men or things at first sight.

translation: There is no thing which does not cause another to exist.
There is no butcher that does not slaughter.
englishEquivalent: Every man to his trade.

translation: One ages every night one lives.
englishEquivalent: Time fleeth away without delay.

kikuyu: Gũtiri ita ithiagwo na gitete kĩa njohĩ no gia ũcũrũ
translation: No war has been fought by men carrying a calabash of ‘njohĩ’ but of ‘ũcũrũ’.
explanation: ‘Njohĩ’ is an inebriating drink brewed out of sugar-cane. ‘Ũcũrũ’ is a kind of thin porridge made by boiling millet-flour in water. This gruel is supposed to be highly nourishing and therefore suitable for long journeys or hard fighting; while the sugar-cane beer by inebriating the warriors makes them weak and easy prey to the enemy.
englishEquivalent: Out of temperance comes strength.

kikuyu: Gũtiri mbura ĩtarĩ na gitonga kiayo
translation: There is no rain which does not enrich someone.
englishEquivalent: It is an ill wind that blows nobody good.

kikuyu: Gũtiri mũciĩ ũri kahĩĩ ũtakarugwo mũtwe
translation: In every family where there is a son, the head of an ox, goat or ram is cooked to be eaten by him with his friends.
explanation: They use the proverb to mean that ordinarily a son gives his parents more trouble than a daughter, or that in every family parents do not lack troubles.
englishEquivalent: There is a black sheep in every family.

translation: There is no difference between the thief and the looker-on.
Nobody entering a hut pays for the heat he will enjoy in it.
explanation: Only the owner of the hut had the drudgery of carrying home the firewood: the visitor does not know the cost of the fire he is enjoying. Metaphorically the proverb is used to say that he who enters a house cannot realise the troubles of the occupants.
englishEquivalent: None knows the weight of another’s burden.

kikuyu: Gũtirĩ mündũ ũĩ haria egũthĩĩ no haria ekuuma
translation: Nobody knows where he goes, but only whence he comes.
englishEquivalent: No one can see into the future.

kikuyu: Gũtirĩ mündũ wendaga gũtũngana na nyoni njũru
translation: Nobody wants to meet an ill-omened bird.
explanation: To the Kikuyu many birds foreshadow calamity. The cry of the owl forebodes mishap. If the owl cries, perched on the top of a hut, the oldest man in that village will die very soon. If someone, about to make a journey, hears the cry of any bird of ill-omen, he must not start on any account.
englishEquivalent: Nobody seeks his own ruin.

translation: There is no man that cannot become an orphan.
englishEquivalent: No flying from fate.

kikuyu: Gũtirĩ mündũ wonaga wega wake, no kuonwo wonagwo
translation: Nobody can see his own goodness: it can be seen only by others.
There is no pleasure (however little it may be) that does not cause one’s cheeks to tremble.
explanation: The Kikuyu consider the cheek trembling an expression of joy.
englishEquivalent: A little pleasure is nevertheless a pleasure.

translation: No day dawns like another.
englishEquivalent: Every day brings a new light.

kikuyu: Gūtiri mūtumia wenjagirwo mbūi kwa nyina
translation: No married woman will have her white hair shaved at her mother's.
explanation: The Kikuyu girls go around with bald heads which they get periodically shaved by their relations. So the woman, who by being married has left her house and relations, will never be shaved at her mother's.
englishEquivalent: Once sold, ever sold.

translation: The son does not cut his finger in cutting meat for his father.
englishEquivalent: Sons are stingier than their parents.

translation: There is no partridge which does not know its own way of scratching.
No partridge is small when it claws the soil.
englishEquivalent: Every one can do great good or evil according to his possibilities.

translation: No prepotent man will insult other people for two consecutive seasons.
englishEquivalent: Prepotence comes quickly to an end.

translation: Meat has no choice morsel.
englishEquivalent: When distributing the meat or anything else one must not favour any one person.

translation: There is no nice bird in the millet.
explanation: Millet is one of the staple crops of the Kikuyu. They protect it from birds by building pulpit-like huts in which boys or women stand to frighten them whilst the harvest is ripening.
englishEquivalent: Even sugar itself may spoil a good dish.

translation: Nobody is born wise.
Nobody returns where he got his finger bitten.

kikuyu: Gütiri ūkagia ūtūmī atari na haria akuratha
translation: Once bitten twice shy.
There is a reason for everything.
Nobody walks with another man's gait.

kikuyu: Gütiri ūragio ni ūtonga no ūkia
translation: There is nothing without a cause.
All things have a beginning.
Nobody grumbles at being rich, all at being poor.

kikuyu: Gütiri ūru ūtūraga, no wega ūtūraga
translation: There is no mischance you are guaranteed against.
There is no bow without its meat.
There is no name which cannot distinguish a child.
englishEquivalent: Every bird is known by its feathers.

translation: There is no location which discusses its affairs in the same way as the other does.
englishEquivalent: Every man in his way.

translation: A man is poor not because he scorns possessions, but because he possesses nothing.
englishEquivalent: Sour grapes, as the fox said when he could not reach them.

kikuyu: Gũtiri wa nda na wa mũgongo
translation: There is not the son of the front and the son of the back.
explanation: The Kikuyu mothers carry a baby on the back if they have only one. If they have two, one is carried in front and the other on the back. Of course the one carried near the breasts can suck oftener than the other. That is why they say this is the favourite one.
englishEquivalent: Parents should have no Benjamin.

kikuyu: Gũtiri wiriraga agikuua, eriraga akiiga thi
translation: Nobody grumbles while carrying a load, but when he has laid it down.
explanation: The proverb means that nobody hates to be rich but all hate to become poor; or that nobody refuses to command , though all are sorry when they have to give up the command.

translation: Everybody regrets not what he leaves but what he does not find (when he comes back).

kikuyu: Gũtiri witaga ithe wa ūngĩ baba
translation: Nobody calls another’s father ‘dad’.
To forget a strong man who could help you is the same as to scorn him.
To forget is the same as to throw away.
The man that serves is not prevented from being served in turn.
englishEquivalent: Every dog has its day, and every man his hour.

translation: The day is for working, the night is for resting.
englishEquivalent: There is a time to wink as well as to see.

translation: To seek a woman to the belly.
explanation: The expression is used when they look for something to eat.
englishEquivalent: To go foraging.

translation: Some soldiers are only soldiers when talking.
explanation: A good friend is a treasure. A good action reaps another.
englishEquivalent: One good turn deserves another.

kikuyu: Handĩ ha njuguna na ha mugi hatiganaie
translation: The place to use the club and the arrow are not the same.
englishEquivalent: Everything has its place.

translation: In the presence of elderly people one must not pour water.
explanation: Nobody is allowed to be foul-mouthed specially when elderly people are present.
englishEquivalent: Old age is honourable.

kikuyu: Haro ni ya muka ũri ũlii
translation: Quarrelling is peculiar to the woman who has got male children.

kikuyu: Haro ni ya mūka ũri thiri
translation: Quarrelling is peculiar to the woman who has debts.
englishEquivalent: A woman in debt is quarrelsome.

translation: Resist the beginnings.
englishEquivalent: Small faults indulged are little thieves that let in great.

translation: A wily person does not walk on dry leaves (for they would betray his presence).
Strength does not correspond with courage.
Strength has nothing.
englishEquivalent: Strong people are not necessarily rich people.

translation: When hyenas go away jackals rejoice.
englishEquivalent: Little dogs begin to eat when big ones have eaten enough.

kikuyu: Hiti itaga iria ingi ya mũtiri
translation: The hyena calls another hyena worse than itself.
englishEquivalent: The pot calling the kettle black.

kikuyu: Hiti yugaga arũme ni ogi, monaga gicinga ngwatiro
translation: Hyena says that men are wise because they know how to hold a firebrand.
explanation: A story told by the Kikuyu says that one night a hyena entered a hut to eat the goats. The owner wakened by the noise, took hold of a firebrand to scare it out. The beast tried to do the same, but not knowing how to handle firebrands it scorched its paws.
englishEquivalent: There is a right and a wrong way of doing everything.

kikuyu: Hiti ndiriaga mwana, na mũĩ ũria ũĩ ngoroku
translation: The hyena does not eat its baby, and you know how insatiable it is.
englishEquivalent: No mother is so wicked but loves her children.

translation: Vultures arrive at the place where the goat is slaughtered.
englishEquivalent: Where the carcase is, the ravens will gather.

kikuyu: Hũngũ ĩgithii ĩgũrũ ndiatigire thi kũri kwega
translation: The vulture perches on the trees because it does not feel sure on the ground.
To eat much leaves you with a swollen belly.
englishEquivalent: Enough is as good as a feast.

translation: The abyss laughs at the plain.
englishEquivalent: Every man thinks his own geese swans.

translation: The cow has a bad delivery though her owner is present.
englishEquivalent: Misfortunes may come in spite of watchfulness.

translation: The good milking cow is praised after her death.
englishEquivalent: A friend is never known till needed.

translation: The cow is given a present when her calf is carried away.
englishEquivalent: When one thing distresses you, another consoles you.

translation: The ox that claws the ‘kĩara’ will die.
explanation: ‘Kĩara’ is the dunghill you will find in every Kikuyu

translation: The ox that feeds itself does not spoil its skin.
The animal rambling in the stable makes the sleeping ones rise too.
englishEquivalent: Ill examples are like contagious diseases.

translation: The ram that is shown around is not fat.
explanation: A really fat ram will easily find a buyer and does not need to be carried around and shown in the markets.
englishEquivalent: Good ware makes a quick market.

translation: The cimex lives in the firewood and still it reaches its full growth.
englishEquivalent: Where there is a will there is a way.

kikuyu: Īrī gūciarīra riūa-ini yongithagiria o ho
translation: The cow that drops her calf in the sun feeds it there too.
englishEquivalent: One likes the place where one does well.

kikuyu: Īrī gūkūra īriagwo īguku nī aka
translation: The hump of the ox that has grown old must be eaten by women.
explanation: The hump is a choice morsel for young men when the ox is young. But if it is old women must eat it.
englishEquivalent: Rubbish is women's portion.

translation: The ox which has grown old has no admirer.
englishEquivalent: Nobody looks after elderly people.

translation: The flea troubles him who has got it in his ear.
Nobody gathers firewood to roast a thin goat.
englishEquivalent: Poor people have no friends.

translation: There is no tree which a panting animal would not cling to.
englishEquivalent: A drowning man will catch at a straw.

translation: The ox that ran away cannot be caught.
englishEquivalent: Resist the beginnings.

kikuyu: ĩri kũruga ni ĩgũta, ĩgũtirira ni nguũ
translation: The cooking pot on the fire leaks, when pouring water it is broken.
englishEquivalent: Misfortunes come by forties.

translation: The ox which has no horns, relies for help on the one that has them.
englishEquivalent: He who feels weak relies on the friend he knows is strong.

kikuyu: ĩri mũthece kinya tene ndioyagira ĩngi
translation: The bird who has always possessed a beak, does not pick up for another.
englishEquivalent: Content is more than a kingdom.

kikuyu: ĩri nyite ni mũtego ndithũre gwiteithũra
translation: The animal caught in the trap does not refuse to set itself free.
englishEquivalent: No man likes his fetters, though of gold.

translation: It is he who has got milk that is merciful.
explanation: ‘Milk’ here has the sense of money; possessions. The proverb means that the rich should help needy people, since the poor cannot do it.

translation: The timid ox drinks muddy water.
explanation: He goes to the river only when others have come away leaving the water dirty.
englishEquivalent: Faint heart never won fair lady.

translation: He who goes around with his body upright, later on will go crawling.
englishEquivalent: Young today, old tomorrow.

translation: To blame the wind for the rain that does not fall.
englishEquivalent: It refers to boasting people who try to make silly excuses for themselves.

kikuyu: ĩtari thahu igunagwo ni makoro ma njira
translation: The man who has no impurity will be helped even by the peels he sees on the road.
explanation: There are many ways by which a Kikuyu can contract impurity and he fears the baneful effects which will follow it. That is why a man able to avoid all legal uncleanness is said to be so lucky.
englishEquivalent: God helps honest people.

translation: The goat slaughtered for a man who is sick now, finds another who was sick long before.
englishEquivalent: God cures and the doctor takes the fee.

translation: The sky is heavy with rain, but rain does not come.
explanation: It refers to people who are always promising great things which they never do.
englishEquivalent: Great boast, small roast.

translation: A plant loses its blossom as soon as it bears fruit.
englishEquivalent: Woman's beauty is spoilt by maternity.

kikuyu: Igai ria mûtündũ ritigiragia kiriti kiunwo
translation: A branch of ‘mûtündũ’ does not hinder the division of a field.
explanation: ‘Mûtündũ’ is a small tree growing in the bush.
englishEquivalent: It is not used by the natives, except as firewood.

translation: The tooth laughs with the lance.
explanation: It means that often a person plays with his enemy.
englishEquivalent: The cat plays with the mouse.

translation: Young sugar-cane gives no beer.
englishEquivalent: There is no putting old heads on young shoulders.

translation: Great haste breaks the yam tuber (instead of taking it out whole).
englishEquivalent: Haste trips up its own heels.

translation: Boys and sugar-cane grow up as enemies (because boys are all the time eating sugar-cane).

kikuyu: Ihiga riega ritiringanaga na thio njega
translation: A good millstone does not meet a good miller.
englishEquivalent: Good husband and good wife seldom meet.

translation: The foot and the earth cannot help meeting.
Old people’s walking teaches young ones to walk.
englishEquivalent: That that comes of a cat will catch mice.

translation: One can lose four and eight.
englishEquivalent: All covet all lose.

translation: Stolen things bring in misfortune.
englishEquivalent: Ill-gotten goods seldom prosper.

translation: Riches are found in cultivating together.
englishEquivalent: Many hands make light work.

kikuyu: Irīaga na mbugi kūri na ūgwati
translation: The goats pasture with bells hanging from their necks in order not to stray.
If the first goat goes lame, those that follow will not reach the pasture.
englishEquivalent: Ill examples are like contagious diseases.

translation: Candidates for circumcision after washing do not return to warm themselves at their father's (but go straightway to the place of the ceremony to show their courage).
englishEquivalent: In things that must be it is good to be resolute.

translation: The food that is in the mouth is not yet in the belly.
englishEquivalent: Do not cry herrings till they are in the net.

translation: When the food is cooked there is no need to wait before eating it.
What is in Masai is not in Kikuyu.
englishEquivalent: There is many a slip 'twixt the cup and the lip.

translation: The pit allows the grass to fall in.
explanation: The proverb alludes to the pits the Kikuyu used to dig for trapping wild animals. These pits were covered with sticks over which, as well as over the borders, they put a layer of grass. Since this grass often fell in the pit through the spaces between the sticks, so they say that often one falls into the pit dug by himself.
englishEquivalent: Hoist with his own petard.

translation: Fools rejoice for a bad thing.
englishEquivalent: A fool will laugh when he is drowning.

translation: Cooked food is not sold for goats (but is given to friends, visitors and pilgrims).
englishEquivalent: God helps the poor for the rich can help themselves.

translation: The war of the eyes never comes to an end.
englishEquivalent: The eye is never satisfied with seeing.

translation: The war that has no unity will make no prey.
Other’s ornaments tire one’s neck.
englishEquivalent: Do not wear borrowed plumes.

translation: When ‘ithare’ is uprooted ‘mūgumo’ grows in its place.
explanation: ‘Ithare’ is a kind of cane growing on the river banks. The Kikuyu say it is of no use. ‘Mūgumo’ is a kind of fig tree (Ficus Hochstetteri) which does not grow except leaning on another tree or twisting around it like a creeper.
englishEquivalent: This is why they think that the ‘mūgumo’ is worse than the ‘ithare’.

translation: A fair daughter's father has no ears.
explanation: The father who wants to marry his daughter to the best among the young men who crowd his hut to woo her, turns a deaf ear on their foul words.
englishEquivalent: Few men will be better than their interest bids them.

translation: A joke must not hit the belly.
explanation: The proverb means that there must be a limit also in joking.
englishEquivalent: The jest is tolerable, but to do harm by jest is insufferable.

translation: For a jest one should not take the arrow out of the quiver.
From a jest comes a strife.
englishEquivalent: Jests, like sweetmeats, have often sour sauce.

translation: A joke can break the ear ring.
englishEquivalent: An ill-timed jest has ruined many.

translation: A trick is not an arrow.
englishEquivalent: Good jests bite like lambs not like dogs.

translation: Two rich persons do not wish each other a bird of ill omen.
englishEquivalent: Dog will not eat dog.

translation: Rich people cook their food in a potsherd.
englishEquivalent: The tailor's wife is worst clad.

translation: The village which has got a whetstone does not blunt the knife.
explanation: The sense of the proverb is that if in a village there is a good whetstone it does not mean that the villagers should

translation: A slaughter-house is not without a little blood.
englishEquivalent: Touch pitch, and you'll be defiled.

kikuyu: Kaana ka ngari gakunyaga ta nyina
translation: The son of the leopard scratches like its mother.
englishEquivalent: Like father like son.

translation: The baby nursed by its grand-mother can never be corrected.
One finger does not kill a louse.
englishEquivalent: Union is strength.

kikuyu: Kagwaci ka mwana wene noko kahoragia mwaki
translation: It is always the potato of another family's boy that extinguishes the fire.
explanation: The proverb alludes to the custom of roasting potatoes in the embers of a dying fire.
englishEquivalent: Nobody calls himself rogue.

translation: The stream does not pass over an old stone (through respect to its age).
englishEquivalent: Old age is honourable.

translation: The hunter's son knows how to hunt.
explanation: Like father, like son. purposely blunted their tools in order to whet them. The time will come when the whetstone will have to be used.
englishEquivalent: Every thing is good in its season.

kikuyu: Kahii kogi ta ithe kabaritaga ta migwi
translation: A son as cunning as his father knows the arrows like his father.
englishEquivalent: Like carpenter like chips.

translation: A knife and a shaving-knife are alike.
explanation: The proverb means that if you do not have something you need, you will have something you can use instead.
englishEquivalent: Necessity is the mother of invention.

kikuyu: Kahii karathime kariaga nyama cia kinandu
translation: The blessed knife (son) eats of the meat of the ‘kinandu’.
explanation: ‘Kinandu’ is a small calabash used to keep oil, fat and the best morsels of meat. They say that the father will share the contents of the ‘kinandu’ with the most beloved son.

translation: He who is full does not understand what is told (about others’ troubles).
englishEquivalent: Another’s burden does not worry us.

translation: The fed baby plays on its mother’s bed.
The rambling pole-cat leaves its house when there is a banquet.
explanation: The son that leaves his father’s house for liberty’s sake will not share his father’s inheritance.

translation: A little idleness lost a tilled field.
englishEquivalent: A little leak can sink a great ship.

translation: Kamau who is white becomes black.
explanation: ‘Kamau’ is a typical name. The proverb means that there is nothing constant in this world.

translation: A little idleness causes the ruin of the beehive.
explanation: The Kikuyu hang beehives on the branches of the forest trees, and it is their custom to visit them often to make sure that they are all right. For it might happen that if out of idleness one did not see them regularly, one would ultimately find the branch broken, the beehive fallen and the contents spoilt.

translation: Many people together lift up the ‘ndĩrĩ’.
explanation: ‘Ndĩrĩ’ is a heavy wooden mortar in which the Kikuyu women, when brewing beer, crush the sugar-cane.
englishEquivalent: Many hands make light work.

translation: Take an oath only for the hand you slept on.
englishEquivalent: Swear only to that which you know to be true.

translation: The whetstone in a village does not blunt the knife.
englishEquivalent: Every potter praises his own pots.

kikuyu: Kanua karia kariĩre mbeũ noko koragia, ‘ngahanda ki?’
translation: The mouth who ate the seeds asks, ‘Now what shall I plant?’ He sups ill who eats up all at dinner.
Another’s mouth cannot take the oath for you.
englishEquivalent: Every bird must hatch its own eggs.

translation: The mouth is a chink.
englishEquivalent: From the mouth come many futilities.

translation: The mouth sells the head.
englishEquivalent: The tongue talks at the head’s cost.

translation: You spoke (against yourself) with your own mouth.
explanation: It means that one can sometimes condemn oneself in defending oneself.

translation: A small red snuff-box is a welcome.
explanation: The proverb refers to the Kikuyu custom of giving a pinch of snuff to their friends when they meet.

translation: The little bird that flaps its wings too much will spoil them.
englishEquivalent: One must crawl before one can walk.

translation: ‘Kanywanjui’ scratches its thigh.
explanation: ‘Kanywanjui’ is a species of tiny blue bird with a long bill, which sucks nectar from flowers. The proverb means that such birds, although very small, can do everything for their own needs, and do not require others’ help to have their legs scratched.
englishEquivalent: Every man something can.

translation: He who is stricken knows how to defend himself.
englishEquivalent: Scalded cats fear even cold water.

translation: It is not the owner, trampling his own field, that spoils it (but the others).
explanation: The proverb has arisen from the fact that many people if they have a bad harvest, say that it is the fault of other people who walked across their plantations.
englishEquivalent: Nobody calls himself a rogue.

translation: A person will change his mind on something if left to sleep over it.
englishEquivalent: Never leave till tomorrow what you can do today.

translation: Prophet copies a prophet.
englishEquivalent: Like tree like fruit.

kikuyu: Karatũ gatagwo na kũgũrũ kwa mwene
translation: The shoe is made for the foot that will wear it.
englishEquivalent: If the cap fits wear it.

translation: The baby that refuses its mother’s breast, will never be full.
englishEquivalent: Faint heart never won fair lady.

translation: The sleeping dog is turned by a stick; i.e.
explanation: it turns round to bite if disturbed or touched by a stick.
englishEquivalent: Let sleeping dogs lie.

translation: A stupid turtle-dove is sometimes surprised by night for wanting one more grain of castor-oil plant.
englishEquivalent: Time stays not the fool’s leisure.

translation: The mouth that has saliva does not lack words.
explanation: The proverb means that the man who has something to say will say it.

translation: The word that remains in the belly does not mean anything.
englishEquivalent: Tell the truth and shame the devil.

translation: The song that has no leader, goes wrong.
englishEquivalent: No longer pipe, no longer dance.

translation: The elders of the council do not jump over a brook.
explanation: Metaphorically the proverb means that the elders who are to judge a case must not hurry.
englishEquivalent: But it often means that a person like a judge should not do anything undignified.

translation: The food eaten first lasts longest in the stomach.
englishEquivalent: First impressions are most lasting.

translation: The dunghill grows by straws thrown upon it.
englishEquivalent: Every little helps.

translation: A really good thing is ever good.
englishEquivalent: A good tale is none the worse for being twice told.

kikuyu: Kiere kia njira-ini gitigwatagwo ni muura
translation: A grain of millet grown on the road will bear no ears.
explanation: The proverb means both that a promiscuous woman has little hope of bearing children, and that a thing in common use will not last long.
englishEquivalent: A pot that belongs to many is ill stirred and worse boiled.

translation: The thigh is a bubble.
explanation: Thigh means full blooded youth. The proverb is for the young who scorn old people or make wrong use of their strength to sin. It reminds them that youth passes quickly.
englishEquivalent: Young today, old tomorrow.

translation: What is white becomes black.
explanation: The proverb originates in the fact that the Africans are almost white when they are born, but become black by growing.
englishEquivalent: There is nothing constant but change.

kikuyu: Kigina gitininûkagio irio hande itari ngûrû
translation: The seeds kept are not finished before the ripening of the crops planted in the field.
englishEquivalent: Every thing has its time, and that time must be watched.

translation: The argument breaks the strained cord of the bow.
The argument relaxes the bent bow.
The reason crosses even a flooding river.
The club is added to one’s argument.
Having a good argument (in a discussion) is like having riches.
explanation: The five proverbs here above mean that he who can support his views or actions with a strong argument, will go through any difficulty and obtain what he wants.

translation: The fat of the ‘kinandũ’ is not used to anoint a stranger.
explanation: For the meaning of the word ‘kinandũ’ see No. 228.
englishEquivalent: Charity begins at home.

translation: Who prospered with robbed things?
englishEquivalent: Ill-gotten goods seldom prosper.

kikuyu: Kindũ kiũru no kironda, ũndĩ kiri rũa rwa mũhuhi
translation: A sore is a really bad thing; still it means luck to the doctor.
englishEquivalent: It’s an ill wind that blows nobody good.

kikuyu: Kindũ kiũru no mũndũ ethũkitie we mwene
translation: A really bad thing is to hurt oneself wilfully.
englishEquivalent: It is stupid to cut off your nose to spite your face.

translation: The thing you want must be begged from the owner.
explanation: This means that it must not be acquired from other people nor taken without permission.
englishEquivalent: It is not a sin to sell dear, but it is to make measure.

kikuyu: Kindong’o kiariiire maini ũndũ wa kwaga mayũ ma gũkira
translation: The beetle feeds on excrement for it can’t fly high.
englishEquivalent: If thou hast not a capon, feed on an onion.

translation: Any calabash that has got a bottom can stand upright.
explanation: The proverb means that God gives every man what is required by human nature: but it depends on man to exploit such gifts.
englishEquivalent: Every man is the architect of his own fortune.

translation: The head is shaved at its owner's desire.
englishEquivalent: Let every pedlar carry his own burden.

translation: An invalid does not go to two houses to ask for beer (since he cannot move).
englishEquivalent: Old age is honourable.

translation: If a child has sinned all have sinned.
englishEquivalent: One does the blame, another bears the shame.

translation: It is the gridiron that cries (for the slaughtered goat).
explanation: Everyone rejoices when a goat is killed, for each will have his piece of meat; only the gridiron on which the meat is roasted, weeps, i.e.
englishEquivalent: crackles.

kikuyu: Kiriro kiri ituura gitingireka mundu akome
translation: One person weeping prevents all in a village from sleeping.
englishEquivalent: One barking dog sets all the street a-barking.

translation: The forest in the heart cannot be cut down by somebody else.
englishEquivalent: Troubles in somebody's heart cannot be removed by somebody else.

translation: The fool makes other people stop on the road.
englishEquivalent: The fool wastes the time of other people.

kikuyu: Kirimũ kihithaga rwembea-inĩ rwa nyũmba kiĩĩ v gitikuonwo
translation: The fool hides himself under the eaves of the hut and thinks nobody will see him.
englishEquivalent: It refers to foolish people who invent silly excuses to conceal their faults.

kikuyu: Kirimũ gia gwikigia kirũgite kia muciariire
translation: He who feigns to be stupid is more stupid than the stupid-born.
englishEquivalent: None so deaf as those who won't hear.

translation: A fool can even suck the mother after she is dead.
A fool is like a beehive.
explanation: The proverb means that he is a fool who does not look after his own interest, like the beehive which allows itself to be emptied.

kikuyu: Kiringĩri gia aka ni rwenji rükirega
translation: To force a woman to do something she doesn't like is like forcing a blunt shaving-knife to shave.
He who has a sore does not feel sick on account of it.
englishEquivalent: We are blind to our own faults.

kikuyu: Kiruka gia kimbu gitithiragwo ni mung'ũng'ũtũ
translation: All the species of the chameleon family shall always have a protruding backbone.
englishEquivalent: That that comes of cat will catch mice.

translation: Do not force a big thread into a bead with a small hole.
englishEquivalent: Grasp all, lose all.

translation: A wasted thing cannot be eaten.
englishEquivalent: Wilful waste makes woeful want.

kikuyu: Kiũra kiaringio rũũĩ kiugaga nikio kieringia
translation: The frog that was helped across the river, said she had crossed it by herself.
englishEquivalent: Eaten bread is soon forgotten.

translation: Be patient, a desire is no pain.
explanation: The proverb is told to people who long after anything they cannot obtain.

translation: Desires tie.
englishEquivalent: If your desire be endless, your cares will be so too.

translation: An empty bowl is not offered.
explanation: It means that it is better to keep silence than to try to justify oneself by empty excuses.
englishEquivalent: Be silent or speak something worth hearing.

translation: The dry firewood does not despise the wet one coming from the same tree.
englishEquivalent: Dog will not bite dog.

translation: Mother’s dry firewood laughed at the green one (and it did not think that both of them had but one common lot).
englishEquivalent: Today me, tomorrow thee.

translation: Being praised leads to ruin.
englishEquivalent: Praise without profit puts little in the pot.

translation: To tell the beads is not to cut the thread.
englishEquivalent: Do not judge men or things at first sight.

kikuyu: Kũgũrũ kũri mũhu na kũri ime itihanaine
translation: A foot dirty of ashes is not a foot wet of dew (because the former holds firmly, while the latter skids).
The foot goes all the world over.
englishEquivalent: It is perseverance that prevails.

translation: It is he who speaks that profits, not he who is spoken for.

kikuyu: Kūguniwo mwana no ta kūguniwo nyina
translation: To make the son happy is to make the mother happy.
Hurrying is breaking.
Haste makes waste.
To err is human.
One can escape the rocks and perish in the sand.
To beg is not to steal.
Hunger and surfeit do not leave each other.
Riches have wings.
To be black is not to be stupid.
englishEquivalent: Little bodies may have great souls.

kikuyu: Kũma ti kũma ta ihiga, na kuororoa ti kuororoa ta maaĩ
translation: To be hard does not mean to be hard as a stone, and to be soft does not mean to be soft as water.
englishEquivalent: There is a measure in all things.

translation: To harvest is not so difficult as to keep the harvest.
englishEquivalent: Keep some till more comes.

translation: Knowing too much is like being ignorant.
englishEquivalent: Too much breaks the bag.

translation: He knows a place who lives in it.
englishEquivalent: Every man knows his own business best.

translation: Long live my mother and her ugliness.
To become small is not the same as being cut.
To be caught is not to be imprisoned.
englishEquivalent: There is many a slip, 'twixt the cup and the lip.

translation: Some are males (useful people) and some can only fill the gourds (useless people).

kikuyu: Kũri güciara ũru ta kihia güciara na mĩtĩwe
translation: Some good, some bad, as sheep come to the fold.
explanation: There are women who give forth a bad issue, just like the sorghum that bears its fruit on the head (instead of growing it underground like most Kikuyu crops).

translation: One cannot put the 'ndebe' into a broken ear-lobe.
englishEquivalent: 'Ndebe' is the wooden ring put into the pierced ear-lobe

translation: There are people who, like sugar cane, are killed for being sweet.
englishEquivalent: He who makes himself a sheep shall be eaten by the wolf.

translation: There are lucky and unlucky people.
englishEquivalent: The wind of luck is inconstant.

kikuyu: Kūri ūku ūtatumwo, ta wa nyūngũ
translation: There are things, like the earthen pot, which if ever broken can't be repaired.
englishEquivalent: For some evils there is no remedy.

translation: To eat first is not to be a glutton.
To eat much means to spoil one's belly.
englishEquivalent: Too much breaks the bag.

kikuyu: Kūria nai gūtigiragia mündũ akaria wega
translation: To eat bad food (today) does not prevent a person from having good food (tomorrow).
englishEquivalent: Change of fortune is the lot of life.

translation: One does not eat the soil, but the fruit thereon.
The way of eating a debt is paying it.
englishEquivalent: He that gets out of debt grows rich.

kikuyu: Kūriithia ĩmwe ti kwenda kwa mwene
translation: To graze only one goat is not the owner's will.
englishEquivalent: Evils come though we do not want them.

translation: To have come to an agreement does not mean that the agreement may not be broken.
englishEquivalent: The cat and the dog may kiss, yet are none the better friends.

translation: To till the land is to love oneself.
englishEquivalent: Work is well done that is well loved.

translation: It is bad to be a fool.

kikuyu: Kūrūga ti kwega, amu kiūra kioragire ūthoni na irūga
translation: To leap is bad, since the male-frog by his leaping broke up the betrothal.
explanation: The proverb originates in the following fable. One day the male-frog went to his fiancée’s home to arrange the marriage with her father. But as soon as the fiancée noticed the indecorous leaping-posture assumed by the male-frog during the conversation, she refused to marry him. The Kikuyu tell the proverb to express their esteem for decency and modesty.
englishEquivalent: Loquacity storms the ear, but modesty takes the heart.

kikuyu: Kūrua, kūgūrana na kūriha thiri gūtiriragwo
translation: Nobody feels sorry for having been circumcised, for having bought his wife and for having paid his debts.
explanation: The proverb means that there are certain things that leave no regrets.

translation: Being circumcised is like being scalded.
englishEquivalent: This means that the pain of the circumcision is a few minutes’ pain.

translation: Being circumcised is like building the ‘itara’.
explanation: The ‘itara’ is a trellis of twigs suspended a short distance above the fire-place in the Kikuyu hut to prevent sparks from setting fire to the thatched roof. The same word is often used to mean the whole hut. Thus this proverb means that a young man as soon as circumcised, must realise that the years of irresponsibility are over and that he must see about building his hut and starting a new home.
englishEquivalent: A married man must turn his staff into a stake.

translation: A blow does not (always) injure.

kikuyu: Kuma kwa mbaa gũthii kwa heho
translation: To come from rime and go into the bitter cold.
englishEquivalent: To fall out of the frying pan into the fire.

translation: To come out of one’s house means learning.
englishEquivalent: Travel makes a wise man better.

kikuyu: Kwa Mũcũni ni gwateirwo ni mũhitũki
translation: Mũcũni’s house was ruined by the traveller.
explanation: ‘Mũcũni’ is the name of a person who refused hospitality to a passer by. Since hospitality is traditionally sacred among the Kikuyu, they say that this traveller cursed Mũcũni’s house which went to ruin.

kikuyu: Kwa mũnegeni gũkiūra, kwa mũkiri kworire tene
translation: The house of the talkative man perished long after that of the quiet.
englishEquivalent: It is easy for somebody who is friendly to get help from others.

translation: On the way to one’s beloved there are no hills.
Talking is loving one another.
englishEquivalent: Friendship increases by visiting friends.

translation: To talk is not to grumble.
To talk is not to decide.
To start a family is to start troubles.
When a man is married his troubles begin.
To prepare is not to be afraid.
Let him that wants peace prepare for war.
To see for one's self is different from being told.
Words are but wind, but seeing is believing.
To see the crop in the fields is not to eat it.
Trials mean successes.
englishEquivalent: Where there is a will there is a way.

translation: Old fat sings no song.
explanation: This means that he who goes to dance does not anoint himself with rancid fat. The word ‘fat’ is used for ‘beauty, youth’. The proverb means that old folks cannot have admirers as young ones; that old people cannot hope to have more children.
englishEquivalent: Water run by, will not turn a mill.

translation: The smearing begins on one’s face.
explanation: Actually the Kikuyu who smear themselves very often, always begin the anointing on the face, and laugh at people who begin on any other part of the body.
englishEquivalent: There is a time and a way for all things.

translation: Lies are dangerous.
englishEquivalent: Liars have short wings.

translation: Lies are no debt.

kikuyu: Maitho ma andũ matiendaga kindũ kihinju
translation: Men’s eyes do not like to see anything thin.
explanation: The proverb refers to children, oxen and goats.

kikuyu: Maitho ma arũme ti ma irang’a
translation: Men’s eyes are not the eyes of the ‘irang’a’.
explanation: ‘Irang’a’ is an insect with very tiny eyes. The proverb means that the eyes of this insect see very little, while men’s eyes see everything.

translation: Men’s eyes are not like the ‘mambo’.
explanation: ‘Mambo’ are the holes the Kikuyu make in the hides for fastening them to the ground when they dry them in the sun.

kikuyu: Maitho ma ciura matigiragia ng'ombe inyue
translation: The eyes of frogs do not prevent cattle from drinking.
englishEquivalent: Do what thou ought, let come what may.

translation: The eyes which see each other are destined to see each other again.
englishEquivalent: Friendship increases by visiting friends.

translation: Tears are no language.

kikuyu: Marakara ma arime matitütaga ta ma aka
translation: Men's anger does not last so long as women's.
englishEquivalent: Women are as prone to revenge injuries as men to forgive them.

translation: Getting into rage means being proud.
Run by water does not quench the thirst.
englishEquivalent: Water run by, will not turn a mill.

translation: The water that is not yours flows away while you are folding the 'itüma'.
explanation: 'Itüma' is the leaf of a kind of edible arum. Out of these large leaves the Kikuyu used to drink water.

kikuyu: Mathanwa mari kiondo kinwe matiaga gukomorania
translation: Many axes in one basket must hit against each other.
Some people do not like the building of a hut, though they like the 'mürugürio'.
explanation: 'Mürugürio' is a kind of dedication-ceremony held by the witch-doctor to solemnize the completion of a new hut. On such occasion the owner of the hut distributes beer to his relations and to the people who assisted him in the building.
englishEquivalent: There is scarcity of friendship but not of friends.

translation: They who leave one another forget one another.
englishEquivalent: Out of sight, out of mind.

translation: Slips outnumber falls.
englishEquivalent: Every slip is not a fall.

translation: Days pass quickly.
englishEquivalent: Time fleeth away without delay.

translation: The days are a hurry, i.e.
explanation: go quickly.
englishEquivalent: Time fleeth away without delay.

translation: Not all days are Sundays.
englishEquivalent: Christmas comes but once a year.

translation: The eggs of males do not hatch each other.
explanation: The proverb means both that any man prefers living with a woman rather than with another man, and that there ought not to be two people commanding in one home.
englishEquivalent: Two sparrows upon one ear of wheat cannot agree.

translation: The important things are left in the locker.
explanation: In other words, they are not told to everybody.
englishEquivalent: Tell not all you know.

translation: My stolen or damaged lamb must be replaced by another.
englishEquivalent: An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth.

translation: War is not porridge.
Women's strife has no sheep.
explanation: According to the Kikuyu custom the one that wounds another in a quarrel must pay a sheep as a fine. The proverb means that in women's strifes nobody incurs such a fine, for their quarrels are usually words only.
englishEquivalent: Words are for women, actions for men.

kikuyu: Mbari ya ngeka makorirwo matari meka
translation: They who said ‘I shall do’ became people who had done nothing.
englishEquivalent: Never leave that till tomorrow which you can do today.

translation: The mouse finishes the hide by gnawing.
englishEquivalent: Little strokes fell great oaks.

translation: The future is not so much regretted as the past.

kikuyu: Mbere ni gikeno thutha ni maithori
translation: Tears follow joy.

kikuyu: Mbere no mbere thutha no mūgiano
translation: Before is before: afterwards there is nothing but repining.
englishEquivalent: Resist the beginnings.

translation: Many buffaloes are no meat.
englishEquivalent: If you run after two hares, you will catch neither.

translation: A small flower has no smell.
englishEquivalent: A little barrel can give but little meal.

translation: The goat is attracted by salt.
englishEquivalent: The bait not the hook catches the fish.

translation: No alarm is shouted for a goat (because it is not a dangerous beast).
englishEquivalent: Do not waste time and money on unworthy things.

translation: The goat and the child are not insulted (because they cannot defend themselves).
One can always find the goat to pay the penalty for having defecated in another's house.
explanation: According to Kikuyu customs he who defecates in another's house is liable to be fined a goat. The proverb means that he who incurred such penalty will contrive to find the means to pay it.
englishEquivalent: Necessity sharpens industry.

translation: A chattering goat does not keep its tongue.
explanation: The word 'goat' is here used instead of 'people'.
englishEquivalent: A fool may ask more questions in an hour than a wise man can answer in seven years.

translation: The best part of another's goat is the car.
explanation: The proverb means that a stranger coming in when a slaughtered goat is distributed, must not expect to be given a choice morsel, but rather an inferior part like an ear. Metaphorically the proverb means that a prudent person keeps for himself and his family the best parts of anything instead of giving them away to his visitors and friends.
englishEquivalent: Charity begins at home.

translation: The goat which eats ashes does not hide its habit.
explanation: The Kikuyu live under the same roof as their animals. So if any goat forms the habit of leaving its place and coming to lick ashes at the fire, it will soon be discovered.
englishEquivalent: In the same manner the vices of the wicked will soon be known.

translation: An old goat does not sneeze without cause.
explanation: The proverb means that old folks speak the truth and do not speak without a reason.
englishEquivalent: Old dogs bark not for nothing.

translation: Goats are not bananas (which are given for nothing).
englishEquivalent: There are no gains without pains.

kikuyu: Mbũri ya ngĩa yaringĩrĩra no ũguo bata ũringagĩrĩra
translation: When the poor man's goat is about to kid, then the need drops also.
explanation: The proverb means that if a man rejoices because his goat is going to kid and so increase his property, a sudden need might force him to sell his goat.
englishEquivalent: Count not your chickens before they be hatched.

kikuyu: Mbu ya arũme ifikagio ni athamaki
translation: Men's alarm-shouts are answered by the elders.
explanation: The proverb means that if the alarm is shouted only by women one can make light of it; but if the alarm is cried by men there exists a real danger. Metaphorically the proverb means that women cannot claim any right of discussing or giving evidence in a court.
englishEquivalent: Let women spin and not preach.

translation: The bell needs its tongue.
explanation: In this proverb the word 'bell' means 'woman', and 'tongue' means 'man'.
englishEquivalent: Wives must be had, be they good or bad.

kikuyu: Mburungo nyinyi ũĩ mũthiomeri ũrugite nene itari
translation: mũthiomeri A trifle well presented becomes more precious than a thing of great value badly presented.
englishEquivalent: It is not the value of a gift that matters but the intentions of the giver.

translation: A distant water does not quench one's thirst.
Be not too proud lest you ruin yourself.
The 'miano' cannot be confused, but the mouth can.
explanation: 'Miano' are the small gourds used by witch-doctors to contain the divining stones. The proverb means that the divining stones cannot fail to tell the truth, though it may happen that the witch-doctor does not tell it.
englishEquivalent: God cures and the doctor takes the fee.

translation: The words are the odour of the heart.
englishEquivalent: The tongue ever turns to the aching tooth.

translation: Two hides are not laid out at the same time.
englishEquivalent: One cannot be in two places at once.

kikuyu: Migũire ya ngũ na ya migogo ti imwe
translation: The fall of branches and that of big trees are not the same.
Speaking in a whisper is followed by hiding (in order to steal).
explanation: The proverb means that people who whisper are probably arranging something evil.
englishEquivalent: Beware of a silent dog and still water.

kikuyu: Mitheko ĩtarĩ githimi yumaga kanua-ini ka irimũ
translation: Laugh without measure comes out of fools' mouths.
englishEquivalent: The laughter of fools.

translation: One's pocket is not a repository (in which all people can put their hands).
explanation: Pocket means in this case home affairs.
englishEquivalent: Scald not your lips in another man's pottage.

translation: The hand has not to be put into another's pocket.
englishEquivalent: Scald not your lips in another man's pottage.

translation: He who is in necessity does not feel ashamed (to ask for help).
A cob of maize can knock down a giant.
englishEquivalent: A small leak will sink a great ship.

translation: It is he who travels that finds the tusk.
englishEquivalent: God helps those who help themselves.

translation: Yaws is caught through friendship.
explanation: The proverb means that just as the disease is contracted by contact with infected people, so bad habits are acquired by consorting with bad people.
englishEquivalent: Who keeps company with a wolf will learn to howl.

translation: He who looks for another must find him.
englishEquivalent: He who will seek may find.

translation: He who walks with a mangy man becomes mangy.
englishEquivalent: He who keeps company with a wolf will learn to howl.

translation: Parents are merciful.

kikuyu: Mūciari ndairagio ngoro ni kimira kia mwana wake
translation: Parents do not feel sick when wiping the mucus from their child's nose.
Parents do not take away the earth that covers the root of the sugar cane.
englishEquivalent: As a good farmer does not uncover the roots of the

translation: Parents are proud of their children.
The house is not ruled by him that did not build it.
englishEquivalent: Mind your own business.

translation: The house is for sleeping in by night, not for staying in by day.
englishEquivalent: There is a time for all things.

translation: The house which has goats does not lack miscarriages.
englishEquivalent: Who has land, has war.

translation: The strong smell (of roasting meat) causes the hyena to break its leg.
englishEquivalent: Hasty climbers have sudden falls.

translation: He who advises a fool does not lay down his ‘mūthīgī’.
englishEquivalent: ‘Mūthīgī’ is the staff of the elders.

translation: One man alone in a tribunal can say nothing, i.e.
englishEquivalent: can take no decision.

translation: A slanderer has no peaceful home.
englishEquivalent: Slander flings stones at itself.

kikuyu: Mūgambo ũri kūgūa thi nduoyagwo; woyagwo na ũngĩ
translation: A word that has fallen to the ground cannot be picked up: it is picked up by another.
englishEquivalent: Time and words can never be recalled.

translation: A word given must not be retaken.
He that broils two maize cobs (at the same time) burns one of them.
englishEquivalent: Who hunts two hares leaves one and loses the other.

translation: A broken necklace cannot be made whole again.
englishEquivalent: A broken friendship may be soldered, but will never be sound.

kikuyu: Mũgathi wa kuona ũteaga wa mwene
translation: The necklace found makes you lose your own, too.
englishEquivalent: Ill-gotten things seldom prosper.

translation: The foreigner evacuates in the cemetery (for he does not know the place and its customs).
One does not give any beer to a foolish visitor.
explanation: The proverb means both that it is not honourable for the host to give hospitality to a fool, and that it is silly to give beer to a fool since he does not enjoy it.
englishEquivalent: He is not the fool that the fool is, but he that with the fools deals.

translation: A guest does not eat as much as he wants; i.e.
englishEquivalent: he must not be greedy.

translation: The guest is like a river, i.e.
explanation: he passes quickly.
englishEquivalent: Fish and guests smell at three days old.

translation: He who harvests by night, reaps chaff.
englishEquivalent: There is a time for all things.

translation: He who has been advised is wise.
englishEquivalent: A man forewarned is forearmed.

kikuyu: Mũgiri rwa kũnyitūra agirire rwa kũnyitia
translation: One can cause the illness which he wanted to cure.
englishEquivalent: The cure may be worse than the disease.

translation: He who irritates will be scratched.
englishEquivalent: Let sleeping dogs lie.

translation: One trunk does not close a river.
englishEquivalent: One flower makes no garland.

translation: The she-sheep can break the cooking pot, and still she has no horn.
explanation: Cooking pot means here an affair of great importance.
englishEquivalent: The meaning of the proverb is that a fool can spoil wise people's affairs.

translation: A field begins to become a wilderness from a side; i.e.
explanation: from a small place.
englishEquivalent: A little neglect may breed a great mischief.

kikuyu: Mũgũnda wa mwere ũmenyagwo na ngetho
translation: One knows a field of millet from its crop.
englishEquivalent: The tree is known by its fruits.

translation: Another's field is not praised.
explanation: The proverb refers to the fact that the Kikuyu when they are drunk imagine themselves very rich, and so become proud of others' riches.

translation: The man who buys something at a place near by is like the man who is given something.
englishEquivalent: That is little esteemed that costs little.

kikuyu: Mũgũi ũtarĩ wa awa ni ũkündembũrĩra thiaka
translation: The arrow which is not my father's, pierces my quiver.
englishEquivalent: Ill gotten goods seldom prosper.

translation: He who pays another with his own things, does not bleed.
explanation: The proverb means that one spends his money willingly when he needs help.

translation: He who stands close to his things does not lose them.
englishEquivalent: The master's eye makes the horse fat.

translation: The messenger of peace has no two knives (presents).
englishEquivalent: Messengers should neither be beheaded nor hanged.

translation: He who plants is not he who eats.
englishEquivalent: Man proposes, God disposes.

translation: The one with diarrhoea must look for a bush.
englishEquivalent: Let him that is cold blow the coal.

translation: He who is spoken to at both ears does not understand.
englishEquivalent: Too much consulting confounds.

translation: A liar does not laugh (for if a liar laughs when he tells a lie he is not believed).

kikuyu: Mūhenia ago oigaga mūrimū ūri gūthira
translation: He who would deceive the witch-doctors says that his illness is finished.
englishEquivalent: Hide nothing from thy minister, physician and lawyer.

translation: The deceived has many more days than the deceiver.
englishEquivalent: Liars have short wings.

translation: The deceived is not so cunning as the deceiver.
He who receives must not measure.
englishEquivalent: Do not look a gift horse in the mouth.

kikuyu: Mũhikana na kũria ahikanaga na gũitwo
translation: He who takes his food in a hurry, is also choked in a hurry.
englishEquivalent: Haste makes waste.

translation: He who hastens eats money; i.e.
explanation: wastes his money.
englishEquivalent: Haste makes waste.

translation: He who is in hurry sews a garment (whereas he should mend the old one).
englishEquivalent: Haste is waste.

translation: A clan is not a wall (which can be destroyed).
explanation: The Kikuyu are very keen on keeping distinction between one clan and the other.
englishEquivalent: That is why they say that clandistinction cannot be cancelled.

translation: He who is quiet has no troubles.
He that has been beaten in a quarrel does not sleep in the court-yard.
englishEquivalent: Scalded cats fear even cold water.

translation: He who is surfeited calls the hungry one glutton.
englishEquivalent: It is easy preaching to the fasting with a full belly.

translation: The thief makes the poisoner change his residence.
explanation: The proverb comes from the following story. A witchdoctor intended to poison a thief. But the thief always managed to steal the poison and the witch-doctor had to find a fresh home.

kikuyu: Mũici na kĩhiĩ atigaga kieha kiarua
translation: He who robbed in company with a boy, will live in fear until the boy is circumcised.
englishEquivalent: What children hear at home soon flies abroad.

kikuyu: Mũici na mündũ muka atigaga kieha akua
translation: He who robbed in company with a woman, will live in fear until she dies (for a woman cannot keep a secret).
englishEquivalent: Woman conceals only what she knows not.

translation: The thief cannot keep fit, because his stools contain undigested food.
explanation: The proverb means that a thief, who eats his food in a hurry and with the fear of being caught, cannot enjoy good health.
englishEquivalent: Ill-gotten things seldom prosper.

kikuyu: Mũici ũri hunyũ arindagira ũri maguta
translation: An ugly thief is more likely to be caught than one smeared with fat: i.e.
explanation: carefully dressed. The proverb means that a robber who cannot dissemble will soon be discovered, while the thief who can sham, will continue to flourish.

kikuyu: Mũici ũtari mũnyite ni mũria gake
translation: The thief who has not been caught eats of his own.
explanation: The proverb means that stolen goods belong to the thief if he is not caught.

kikuyu: Mũici wa mũthenya ni oio, na wa ũtukũ ni oio
translation: He who robs in the day is known, and he who robs in the night is known, too.
englishEquivalent: What is done by night appears by day.

translation: The big thorn laughs at the small one.
englishEquivalent: The greatest thieves punish the little ones.

translation: A cousin does not ask and is not refused anything (because he is a member of the kindred).
A cousin is not denied a meal.
englishEquivalent: Both proverbs mean: Charity begins at home.

translation: He who stays near a corpse cannot help weeping.
To stay together is to know each other.

kikuyu: Mũikari mūĩ gitina niwe ūĩ kiria thambo ūriaga
translation: He who stays at the foot of the tree knows what ‘thambo’ eat.
explanation: ‘Thambo’ are the black ants which live and nest on the trees. The proverb means that nobody knows the affairs of a home, society, etc. better than he who lives or has a part in it.
englishEquivalent: Every man knows his own business best.

kikuyu: Mũikari na hunyũ ndakoragwo onete maguta akarega kwīhaka
translation: He who is ugly, is not so because he refused to smear himself with fat (but rather because he had no fat to smear himself with).
englishEquivalent: We are but what God made us.

translation: He that shoots an arrow does not know whom he will hit.
englishEquivalent: You know not where a stone may light.

translation: He on whom fortune has frowned cannot live long.
The man overwhelmed by another’s arguments does not return to discuss matters.
englishEquivalent: Once bitten, twice shy.

translation: He who keeps good hours is not surprised by night.
englishEquivalent: Early to bed, early to rise, make a man healthy, wealthy and wise.

translation: A woman that hangs about does not lack children.
explanation: The proverb refers to the married women who, failing to have children of their husbands’, go around looking for other men.

translation: One returns to the old wife when the young one dies.
englishEquivalent: Half a loaf is better than no bread.

kikuyu: Mũka ũrĩ kironda ainagira gitiro ihũgo
translation: The woman who has a sore dances on the outskirts.
englishEquivalent: A guilty conscience needs no accuser.

translation: The woman who has children does not desert her home.

kikuyu: Mũka wa mwathi ahingaga na kũgũrũ etereire kiguru-mũki oke
translation: The hunter's wife, awaiting her husband's return, closes the door only with her foot; i.e.
explanation: she leaves the door unbolted so that her husband may enter more quickly with his prey.

kikuyu: Mũkarire ni ũmwe no mũrarire ti ũmwe
translation: To stay together is not the same as to have the same type of life.
englishEquivalent: People often agree in words but not in judgement.

translation: You will pass through the ear-holes.
explanation: The Kikuyu pierce the lobes and the upper part of their ears to put wooden sticks in the holes as an ornament . They use this proverb referring to people attempting to perform impossibilities. It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the Kingdom of Heaven.

translation: He that milks is not he that holds the calf.
englishEquivalent: Every man to his own job.

translation: The miser denies food to him who is surfeited.
explanation: The proverb refers to stingy people who deny some help to others who would in turn be the most helpful.

translation: He who gets up early returns early.
englishEquivalent: The early bird catches the worm.

translation: He who ages in the 'githũnũ' is not known by other people how old he is.
explanation: 'Githũnũ' is a dormitory where unmarried people sleep. The proverb means that he who has not hut and no wife will age without having children to tell him how old he is.

translation: Old man, divide, and teach me how to divide.
explanation: This proverb shows how the Kikuyu respected old people, to whom was left the distribution of meat, beer, etc. at all gatherings.
englishEquivalent: Old age is honourable

translation: The woman whose sons have died is richer than a barren woman.
The pot-maker cooks in a pot-herd.

kikuyu: Mũmeni mündũ ũngĩ amwitaaga kiongo kia njau
translation: He who despises another man, calls him 'head of calf'.
explanation: Owing to their esteem for oxen, it is not dishonourable for the Kikuyu to be told he has a head as big as that of an ox.
englishEquivalent: But it is shameful to be called 'head of calf' since the calf is a useless animal.

translation: He who despises another steals even the snuff from his nose; i.e.
englishEquivalent: has no respect for him.

translation: Man counts what he is refused, not what he is given.
englishEquivalent: We are more mindful of injuries than benefits.

kikuyu: Mündũ mūgi ndari mūhere wa ūhoro
translation: A wise man does not need to be told a thing twice.
englishEquivalent: A word is enough to the wise.

translation: The witch-doctor cannot do for himself what he does for others.

kikuyu: Mündũ mūgo wa gwthokia ndari rūa
translation: The witch-doctor who goes to see a patient without being sent for, will not have the hide of the slaughtered goat; i.e.
explanation: will have no reward.
englishEquivalent: Give neither counsel nor salt till you are asked for it.

translation: The witch-doctor of the place is not needed.
englishEquivalent: Never a prophet was valued in his own country.

translation: Woman and sky cannot be understood.
englishEquivalent: Woman, wind and fortune are ever changing.

translation: A woman must not be killed.
explanation: The reasons for this proverb are the facts that the woman is too weak to defend herself and that only the woman can produce children.

translation: A woman is not sent to collect debts.
englishEquivalent: Let women spin and not preach.

translation: The obedient man gets through.
englishEquivalent: Do what thou ought and dread no shame.

translation: Men act promptly.

kikuyu: Mündũ ūrakanyuira niwe ūī karī rita
translation: He that has drunk once, knows that to drink is a pleasure;

kikuyu: Mündũ ũri na ũndũ otaga mwaki na riũa
translation: The man who warms himself at the fire while the sun is shining, does so for some reason.
People who have no goat do not desire meat.
englishEquivalent: 'Sour grapes,' as the fox said when he could not reach them.

kikuyu: Mündũ ũtathiga athinjaga mwati atoindũrũme irigicegũ
translation: He that does not travel slaughters the she-goat as he is ignorant of a ram in his fold; i.e.
englishEquivalent: he is stupid.

kikuyu: Mündũ ũtathiaga oi no nyina ũrugaga
translation: He that does not travel knows only his mother's cooking.
explanation: Both the proverbs mean that he that does not leave his native place will have a very limited knowledge. The world is a great book, of which they who never stir from home read only one page.

kikuyu: Mündũ wa rurugi ourugagwo akerwo niwe wurugana
translation: He who is wont to provoke others, is called a provoker even when he is provoked.
englishEquivalent: A liar is not believed when he speaks the truth.

translation: He who has circumcised me once does not return to do it again.
explanation: The proverb means that he who has erred or has been cheated once, becomes wise and will not be cheated a second time.
englishEquivalent: He who stumbles twice over one stone deserves to break his shins.

translation: One mouth must be changed; i.e.
explanation: it is not good to talk always with the same person nor about the same things.
englishEquivalent: Change of pasture makes fat calves.

translation: Fortune passes.
englishEquivalent: When fortune smiles take the advantage.

translation: Fortune is beyond the bush, i.e.
explanation: the obstacle.
englishEquivalent: He that endures overcomes.

translation: Fortune is not a thing that must surely come.
He who is thirsty goes to the river.
