englishEquivalent: Let him that is cold blow the coal.

kikuyu: Mũra na mündũ ti mũra na hiti
translation: To be robbed by a person is different from being robbed by a hyena.
explanation: The proverb means that if you were robbed by a person, you can hope to be recompensed for the damage; but if a member of your family or a head of your herd has been stolen by a hyena, there is no hope of redress.
englishEquivalent: There are injuries beyond redress.

translation: It is not the killer that moans, but the killed.
He who refuses (to do something) when asked, does not refuse when forced.
He who refuses to obey cannot command.

kikuyu: Mũremwo ni ndiogo olgaga nja ũĩĩ mahaga
translation: He that cannot dance says that the yard is stony.
englishEquivalent: A bad workman complains of his tools.

kikuyu: Mũri kūria ta athi a thatū
translation: Sometimes one eats bad food like the hunters when they are out hunting in the misty season.
explanation: The proverb comes from the fact that hunters, who stay in the forest or in the plain for rather a long time must often be content with cold, raw food.
englishEquivalent: When bread is wanting, oaten cakes are excellent.

kikuyu: Mũria na gati ndoi mũria na kaara ni akũhia
translation: He who eats with a stick does not know that he who eats with the fingers gets scalded.
He who eats cooked food has someone who cooks it for him.
explanation: The proverb means that he who desires a thing sufficiently either can easily have it, or will make efforts to get it.
englishEquivalent: Nothing is impossible to a willing mind.

translation: He is not condemned who eats even unripe maize of his own fields.
englishEquivalent: Every man is a king in his own house.

translation: He who eats alone dies alone.

kikuyu: Mũrimirwo ni ithe ndoi indo irĩ bata
translation: He who has his fields tilled by his father, does not know that things are precious.
englishEquivalent: What costs little is little esteemed.

translation: One must not break the arm of him who tills the fields.
englishEquivalent: Do not kill the goose that lays the golden eggs.

translation: One tiller does not fill the granary.
englishEquivalent: Union is strength.

translation: He that tills the earth is not he that eats (its fruits).
Sweetness does not satisfy hunger.
explanation: The proverb means that pleasures do not quench the thirst for many more pleasures.
englishEquivalent: But it is also used when we should say: ‘Sweet words butter no parsnips.’

translation: Pleasure cannot be communicated.
explanation: The proverb means that he who has any reason for rejoicing, cannot feel unhappy even if his friends or neighbours are grieved.

translation: Pleasure does not last so much as gratitude.
explanation: The proverb means that few virtues are as great as gratitude and that few joys are greater than that of being thanked for a service.
englishEquivalent: Gratitude surpasses all other virtues.

translation: Sweetness eats up itself and
Sweetness brings sorrow.
englishEquivalent: Pleasure stings even though it pleases.

translation: Sweetness spoils teeth.
Sweetness makes the vulture descend from the tree.
englishEquivalent: Beauty draws more than oxen.

kikuyu: Mūrio wa njohi ni ūriūkagwo, no wa indo ndūriūkagwo
translation: The drunkenness of beer passes away, but the drunkenness of wealth lasts forever.
englishEquivalent: Avarice increases with wealth.

translation: He who asks too much will not eat anything.
englishEquivalent: All covet, all lose.

translation: They who live together must be merciful.
englishEquivalent: Bear and forbear is good philosophy.

kikuyu: Mũrimũ ndũri hinya ũgitonya mwiri ta ũkiuma
translation: Illness enters the body with less difficulty than it meets on going away.
englishEquivalent: Misfortunes come on wing and depart on foot.

kikuyu: Mũrimũ wa mücoka nìguo ũragaga mündũ
translation: It is the illness that returns that kills people.
englishEquivalent: Resist the beginnings.

translation: The poisoner cannot stop the effect of the poison.
explanation: The proverb refers to the superstition by which a person who has been poisoned cannot go to his poisoner to have the effect of poison neutralized by his arts but must go to another person, who is called ‘mũrogori’.

translation: He who looks at another’s field sees many more weeds than does its owner.
englishEquivalent: To be blind to one’s own faults.

translation: He who cooks food for men, does not lack big veins, i.e.
explanation: bruises. The proverb means that he who works for a master must do his duty to avoid punishment.
englishEquivalent: Men like facts not words.

kikuyu: Mũrũngũru wa njamba ũtahaga na ime
translation: He who rises early skips in the dew.
explanation: The proverb means that people who get up early finish their work early.
englishEquivalent: The early bird catches the worm.

translation: The ‘mûruri’ does not build.
explanation: ‘Mûruri’ is a forest tree with beautiful red flowers, but yielding very poor timber.
englishEquivalent: All is not gold that glitters.

translation: He who circumcises the boy was a boy, too.
He who circumcises the males was circumcised.
englishEquivalent: The child is father of the man.

kikuyu: Mûtego ti ngoro, ni wathi warera
translation: It is not the trap that counts, but the art of trapping.
englishEquivalent: A good archer is known by his aim, not his arrows.

translation: Both he that chases and he that is chased become tired.
englishEquivalent: Everyone has his own troubles.

kikuyu: Mûthakwa wa athi ndûthiragwo ni gicanjara
translation: The ‘mûthakwa-tree’ will not discontinue to produce branches of only one shape.
englishEquivalent: Like father like son.

translation: The wise man who is not taught is not a wise man.

kikuyu: Mûthinio ni kuona arûga mûthinio ni wagi
translation: He who is troubled by having (property) is better off than he who is troubled by poverty.
He who sends somebody to a witch-doctor on his behalf must believe all he is told.
He who is sought by a man already in the courtyard, has no way of escape.
englishEquivalent: To understand this proverb one must bear in mind that

translation: He that dislikes a person—is he God?
explanation: The proverb means that if anyone is hated by men, he is not necessarily hated also by God.
englishEquivalent: God is just.

translation: He that is lame of heart—unlike him that is lame of foot —cannot be recognized.
englishEquivalent: All is not gold that glitters.

kikuyu: Mũthuri ũtarĩ kahĩ niwe wiragira ngururu
translation: The married man who has no son goes himself to scare away the birds from his harvest.
A dried up tree does not bear a green one.
englishEquivalent: One cannot get blood out of a stone.

translation: The tree falls on the man who stands by it.
A tree which is not intended to be felled, is not aimed at with an axe.
explanation: It is told of people who, devoting themselves to many things at the same time, finish none.
englishEquivalent: Jack of all trades and master of none.

translation: He who leaves a bunch of bananas finds a whole stalk.
englishEquivalent: Give and spend, and God will send.

translation: The man left where there was once a hut, will certainly find something.
He who leaves a white goat will meet another of the same colour.
englishEquivalent: Contentment is above wealth.

translation: Danger makes a man rise from bed.
englishEquivalent: Men in danger need no spur.

translation: Misfortune frustrates one's plans.
englishEquivalent: Man proposes, God disposes.

kikuyu: Mütirima wa kirimũ witirimagia na mūgi
translation: A fool's walking-stick helps the wise man to stand.
explanation: The proverb means that wise people know how to get profit from things that a fool thinks useless.
englishEquivalent: A wise man gets learning from those who have none themselves.

translation: He who lives a long time (in one place) must find what he wants.

kikuyu: Mütumia angikūra atarĩ mwana ndangiona mütahīri maai
translation: The woman that gets old without bearing a child, will have nobody to draw water for her, i.e.
explanation: will have nobody to help her.
englishEquivalent: Children are poor men's riches.

kikuyu: Mütumia na kionje ni ūndũ ūmwe
translation: A woman and an invalid man are the same thing.
englishEquivalent: Words for women, actions for men.

kikuyu: Mutumia ndatūraga mütwe na ndaikagia ndahi ndua
translation: A woman does not split the head (of the slaughtered goat) nor dip the cup into the beer (because both are men's jobs).
englishEquivalent: Let women spin and not preach.

translation: He that hands the hammer is not the same as the man who pulls the bellows.
englishEquivalent: You cannot drink and whistle at the same time.

translation: A blind man does not show another the way.
englishEquivalent: Blind does not lead blind.

translation: He who carries an embassy has no concern in it.
englishEquivalent: Messengers should neither be beheaded nor hanged.

translation: Only one head does not divide a field.
englishEquivalent: Four eyes see more than two.

kikuyu: Mūtwe wa mündũ ūmwe ni ithino
translation: One man’s head is a solitary place.
englishEquivalent: Counsel is not of one.

translation: He who speaks does not know what others will reply.
He who travels sees great things.
explanation: The world is a great book, of which they who never stir from home read only one page.

kikuyu: Muni kiriti niwe ūĩ ūria thina ūigana wa migogo na
translation: nyamũ It is the forest clearer who knows the troubles caused by trunks and animals.
englishEquivalent: Every man knows his own business best.

kikuyu: Mumi na nja oyaga mara kana anyuaga twiri
translation: He that enters a hut either picks up the bowels or drinks twice.
explanation: To understand the proverb one must remember that the Kikuyu huts receive the only scanty light from the low front door. So people who enter a hut where a banquet is being held may either be unlucky and take hold of a piece of bowel instead of a piece of good meat, or may be lucky and be given a couple of drinks.

translation: It is they who have not died in war that start it.

kikuyu: Mwagi maguta oigaga hünyũ ni ūmwe na maguta
translation: He that lacks fat says ugliness is the same as beauty.

kikuyu: Mwagi maguta oigaga ati king'arũ ni ũndũ ũmwe na maguta
translation: He who has no fat (to smear himself with) says that ochre is as good.
explanation: In both these proverbs ‘fat’ means ‘beauty’.
englishEquivalent: ‘Sour grapes,’ as the fox said, when he could not reach them.

translation: Fire is not extinguished by fire.
englishEquivalent: Fire is not to be quenched with tow.

translation: He that begins, is not he that finishes.
englishEquivalent: Judge not of men or things at first sight.

translation: He who receives does not loathe.
englishEquivalent: A gift horse should not be looked in the mouth.

kikuyu: Mwana mũkũrũ na ithe ni hamwe
translation: The eldest son and the father are one thing.
explanation: The proverb means that after the father’s death the eldest son rules.

translation: Only the belly is a good (lucky) child (for its owner takes care of it and never lets it empty).
englishEquivalent: The belly is the commanding part of the body.

translation: The son most loved (by his parents) does not know how to shake his feather head-dress.
explanation: The proverb alludes to the initiation rite, on which occasion a special head-dress composed of ostrich feathers is worn by the candidates. It means that often the young man for whom the parents have bought a costly headdress so that he may look well, does not show any gratitude by wearing it proudly.
englishEquivalent: Things got easily are not appreciated.

translation: The child is not given away without a price.
explanation: The proverb is used especially by a father to the young man wanting to marry his daughter. It must be borne in mind that the Kikuyu girl is not given to her husband, but she is bought by him.
englishEquivalent: No gains without pains.

translation: The son is not beaten when the father is near.
The son need not ask his father for a piece of meat (for a parent spontaneously gives his children the best food).
A child who likes work does not lack one to wash him, i.e.
englishEquivalent: to take care of him.

translation: God tempers the wind to the thorn lamb.

kikuyu: Mwana wa ndigwa niwe ũi kwiera
translation: The baby that has some one to care for it does not dirty itself.

kikuyu: Mwana wa ngari akunyaga ka nyina
translation: Young and old age complete each other.

kikuyu: Mwana wa ngori ndekagira njugiri kũgũrũ
translation: The orphan boy wears no rattles on his feet.

kikuyu: Mwana wa rwendo ariaga nyina na itie
translation: The Kikuyu used to wear rattles on their feet when dancing.
explanation: The proverb has the obvious meaning that the son who

translation: The son of sin does not cease weeping.
englishEquivalent: Sins and debts are always more than we think them to be.

kikuyu: Mwana wa na ithe ndanyuaga muma
translation: The son, whose father is still alive, takes no oath (for his father defends him and if necessary, takes the oath instead of the son).
The youth is a part of the Divinity.
explanation: The proverb originates in the fact that the circumcised Kikuyu youth is greatly respected by women and uncircumcised young men.

translation: The youth who has enough to buy his girl, need not beseech her.
englishEquivalent: Money is the sinew of love as well of war.

translation: He who airs something must air himself first.
englishEquivalent: No gains without pains.

kikuyu: Mwari mwega ahitükira thome wa ngia
translation: A fair girl does not stop at a poor youth's (for he could not buy her).
One does not consult the witch-doctor about a white daughter.
explanation: It is luck for Kikuyu parents to have a daughter with skin whiter than the average.
englishEquivalent: Such a girl will be sold dearer to her husband.

translation: He who talks about others' affairs does not know his own.
A boy is not sent to collect the honey (for he does not know how to collect it).
englishEquivalent: Every man does his own business best.

kikuyu: Mwatūkiria ki? Aca no thũmbĩ na rũhuho
translation: What have you that we have not?
explanation: Nothing but ‘thũmbĩ’ and wind. ‘Thũmbĩ’ is the piece of cloth or leather used to fasten ostrich and other birds’ feathers around the head. The proverb means, ‘There is no news’.

kikuyu: Mwathwo ni nda arũgĩte mwathwo ni ithe
translation: Being ruled by one’s stomach is better than being ruled by one’s father.
Good people are sucked.
englishEquivalent: Cover yourself with honey and the flies will attack you.

translation: He that wants to become rich must till the earth.
englishEquivalent: Sleeping foxes catch no poultry.

translation: He who wants papyrus-ashes burns papyrus.
explanation: Previous to the advent of Europeans, the Kikuyu used papyrus-ashes, which are supposed to be rich in sodium, for cooking purposes.
englishEquivalent: Let him that is cold blow coal.

kikuyu: Mwendi mũhiriga ũtuikane etagia rũrĩmĩ na mbere
translation: ndarũriaga He who wants to cause disagreement within the clan asks for the tongue (of the slaughtered goat) which he was not wont to eat before.
explanation: The tongue of the goat is a choice morsel which belongs by right to the head of the family or clan. The proverb means that he who wants a pretext for quarrelling, asks for something which he cannot be given.

translation: He who seeks evil finds it.
He who wants beauty does not complain (if it costs him some pain).
englishEquivalent: No gains without pains.

translation: He who sells buys.
englishEquivalent: To buy and to sell are both business.

translation: He who is loved receives no refusal.
The barber who shaves badly does not know any other (better) way of shaving.
explanation: The first degree of folly is to think himself wise, the second is to tell others so, the third is to despise all counsel.

translation: The good millet is known at the harvest time.
englishEquivalent: A tree is known by its fruit.

translation: He who waits gets the best food, i.e.
explanation: the biggest potato, the sweetest maize, etc.
englishEquivalent: and can eat better cooked food.

translation: He who wants to dig out a potato does not use a blunt pole.
explanation: The proverb means that he who wants to accomplish something, uses just those means that ensure success.

translation: The frog that compared itself to the ox lost its buttocks.
explanation: There is a fable, that a frog seeing what big buttocks the ox had, thought it could grow as big by swelling. But it burst and so lost buttocks and life.
englishEquivalent: All covet, all lose.

kikuyu: Mwigerero wa ngoro ndũkinyaga no wa Ngai ũkinyaga
translation: What man wants does not reach the goal, only what God wants reaches it.
englishEquivalent: Man proposes, God disposes.

translation: Self defence is not fear.
englishEquivalent: Weapons bode peace.

translation: To obtain what one wants is not a month's job.
englishEquivalent: Time and straw make medlars ripe.

translation: He who lives alone has no quarrel.
englishEquivalent: It takes two to make a quarrel.

translation: He who looks after his own business has no trouble.
He who has no patience will have no hard yams.
explanation: Yams are fully ripe only when they have grown hard. So he who wants to eat a good yam must be patient and wait till it is hard.
englishEquivalent: Everything is good in its season.

kikuyu: Mwiri ti icoya ati ni ũgũtembũka
translation: One's body is not a banana leaf which should be rent.
explanation: The proverb is told to people who threaten to abuse or have abused others.

translation: The body which has blood cannot help being subject to illness.
englishEquivalent: They who would not suffer in this world should not be born in it.

translation: He who revenges himself is bad.
explanation: In taking revenge a man is but even with his enemy; but in passing it over he is superior.

translation: He who takes counsel only from himself meets no hatred.

kikuyu: Mwithinia ndathinũkaga, no mũthinio nĩ athinũkaga
translation: He who is the cause of his own troubles never comes to the end of them; but he who is troubled by others does.
He who sees today does not see tomorrow.
englishEquivalent: Today thee, tomorrow me.

translation: Haste, before the trunk-bridge becomes slippery.
explanation: It must be borne in mind that native bridges consist mostly of only one trunk spanning the two banks of the river.
englishEquivalent: Hence passing on such bridges in wet weather is dangerous.

kikuyu: Nda ĩmwe yumaga mũici na mũrogi
translation: The same womb gives birth to a thief and a poisoner.
The belly is more important than war.
The belly is not a head.
explanation: Into the head you can put as many things as you know without filling it, but you cannot do the same with your belly.

translation: I gave you the beauty of a guinea fowl and you give me the beauty of a francolin.
explanation: The proverb originates in the following fable.
englishEquivalent: Once 79

kikuyu: Ndaregirwo ni ikere ta njagathi ikiregwo ni guoya
translation: I have got no calves as lizards have got no hair.
explanation: Well shaped calves are supposed by the Kikuyu to add a great deal to one's beauty: therefore they are much appreciated.
englishEquivalent: As poor as a church mouse.

translation: The arrow does not age (although it be often used).
englishEquivalent: Good bees never turn to drones.

translation: The long road arrives (at the goal).
explanation: The proverb means that a long but sure way, is better than a short but dangerous one.
englishEquivalent: Fair and softly goes far in a day.

kikuyu: Ndegwa nyinyi ihaicaga ng'ombe na mûtwe
translation: The young bull mounts the cows from the head.
englishEquivalent: Young is the goose that will not eat oats.

translation: Sentences do not curdle like milk.
englishEquivalent: Words and feathers are tossed by the wind.

translation: Good words are those spoken of common accord.
explanation: The proverb means both: 'Friendship is friendship and business is business' and 'A word is enough to the wise'.

translation: The animal that eats slowly can swallow well.
englishEquivalent: He that goes softly, goes safely.

translation: Nobody is forced to build his hut on the pattern of his ‘wakinī’.
explanation: ‘Wakini’ is a person circumcised at the same time— somebody of the same age-group.
englishEquivalent: Every one to his own taste.

translation: The thief does not tread on dry leaves (for they would betray his presence).
The bee does not begin with the comb.
englishEquivalent: A good beginning makes a good ending.

kikuyu: Ndīgūre: Konyū kegūra ni komirie ikwa
translation: Humble yourself: the inhabitants of Konyu were able to grow the yams after humbling themselves.
explanation: The proverb originates in the legend that the people of Konyu, a place in Kikuyu country, who had been at war with their neighbours of Mathira, ceased to be raided and could till their fields in peace, only by submitting.
englishEquivalent: He makes a good war that makes a good peace.

translation: The ox does not become old with strong muscles.
explanation: The proverb means that man cannot expect to age and to retain the vigour of his youth.

translation: The mortar is not filled with juice in the place where it is rolled.
explanation: The proverb means that anything is found useful only in that place and by those people who are in need of it.
englishEquivalent: Everything is good in its own season.

kikuyu: Ndirĩ njega ndiringanaga na mũthĩ mwega
translation: A good mortar never meets a good pestle.
explanation: The proverb means that a good wife rarely meets a good husband and vice versa.

translation: Still water has finished many men.
englishEquivalent: Beware of a silent dog and still water.

translation: I do not want you to stick on to me like beard moss (sticks on the tree).
englishEquivalent: Live and let live.

translation: I do not hate him who sees me so much as him who reveals me, i.e.
explanation: my faults.
englishEquivalent: Nobody is willing to acknowledge he is in fault.

kikuyu: Nditikũ na magũmi, o kũria mũgaitanirira
translation: Nditikũ and Magũmi (go) to the place where you can agree.
explanation: ‘Nditikũ and Magũmi’ are metaphorical names used to mean two quarrelsome people. The proverb is told to disagreeable people, who though warned do not stop their strife.
englishEquivalent: He that cuts himself willingly deserves no balsam.

translation: It is not the meagre (but the fat) ox that breaks its leg.
englishEquivalent: Misfortunes seldom come alone.

translation: A rich evil-doer is worse than a miser
One rich man cannot close the ford; i.e.
explanation: cannot do all he would.
englishEquivalent: No living man all things can.

translation: Do not give your foot the position which ‘Nyakīnyua’ gives.
englishEquivalent: ‘Nyakīnyua’ is used to mean old women, who often sit unbecomingly.

translation: Every little hole of the ear has its little thorn.
explanation: The Kikuyu used to put little sticks or thorns in the pierced upper part of the ear.
englishEquivalent: Every sparrow to its ear of wheat.

translation: Do not torment yourself as you torment the seeds of the broom-tree (which you scatter everywhere without any regard).
Friendship begins with meeting at a road.
Friendship is steps, i.e.
explanation: it consists in going to see one another.
englishEquivalent: Friendship consists in visiting friends.

translation: Many friends make one’s pocket empty.
englishEquivalent: Friends are pick-pockets.

kikuyu: Ndūgū ya mwana īmatagio ni nyina
translation: The friendship of the son is strengthened by his mother.
englishEquivalent: Children’s joys are parents’ joys.

translation: I live alone like a poisoner.
explanation: The proverb illustrates the Kikuyu’s dislike for poisoners and wizards.

translation: I live on saliva like a flea.
englishEquivalent: To live from hand to mouth.

translation: Do not compare death with sleep (because they are not the same).
Do not make home affairs known.
englishEquivalent: Do not wash dirty linen in public.

translation: Do not finish the small ‘ndũma’.
explanation: ‘Ndũma’ are the tubers of an edible arum much cultivated in Kikuyu. The proverb means that one must dig out only the big tubers and leave the small ones to grow new plants.
englishEquivalent: Enjoy the present but think also of the future.

translation: Do not follow me as the ‘njũũ’ follow the locusts.
explanation: ‘Njũũ’ is the name of a kind of passerine bird, which follows locusts to feed on them.
englishEquivalent: God deliver you from a false friend.

translation: The ‘ndũra’ gives forth nothing but thorns.
explanation: ‘Ndũra’ is the name of a thorny tree. The proverb means: One cannot gather figs from thistles.

translation: Darkness shows no wrong path to him who gets what he wants before dark.
englishEquivalent: Early to bed, early to rise, make a man healthy, wealthy and wise.

translation: A blind man does not show another blind man the way.
explanation: Do the blind lead the blind?
englishEquivalent: Do they not both fall into the ditch?

kikuyu: Ndundu ya nyina na mwana ndiringagiririo
translation: It is not fair to attempt to penetrate mother and son's secrets.
Two noisy waterfalls cannot agree (in their tune).
englishEquivalent: Two of a trade seldom agree.

translation: The turtle-dove coos when it has seen its nest.
englishEquivalent: Every bird likes its own nest best.

translation: It is the hyena that howls.
explanation: The proverb is applied to boisterous people.
englishEquivalent: Barking dogs seldom bite.

translation: One can sing the song which precedes the circumcision and not be circumcised.
englishEquivalent: Man proposes, God disposes.

kikuyu: Ni mūguanite ta gikwa na mūkũngũ
translation: You agree like the yam and the tree to which it clings.
englishEquivalent: To be like David and Jonathan.

translation: Somebody may come in higher in dignity than he who was firstly invited.
explanation: The proverb has almost the same meaning as the words of the Gospel: 'When thou art invited to a wedding sit not down in the first seats at the table, lest perhaps one more honourable than thou be invited by him'; etc.
englishEquivalent: Humility often gains more than pride.

kikuyu: Ni ngingo itindaga irĩ theri ti nda
translation: It is the neck that stays without ornament, but not the belly (without food).
The ‘ngaita’ is not eaten unless there is reason.
explanation: ‘Ngaita’ is the very bitter fruit of a shrub, which is taken as an anthelmintic.
englishEquivalent: Medicines are not meat to live on.

kikuyu: Ng’aragu ya mündũ ũngĩ ndingigiria ngome
translation: Other people’s hunger does not hinder me from sleeping.
Arguments are the source of strifes.
englishEquivalent: It takes two to make a quarrel.

translation: Discord breeds scorn.

kikuyu: Ngari ndioĩ gũkunya ni kuonio yonirio
translation: The leopard did not know how to seize its prey: it was taught.
explanation: The Kikuyu say that when the leopard began to kill goats, it did not know how to seize them to kill. One day frightened by the shepherd, it had to leave its prey badly wounded though not killed. From the tree where it had taken refuge it heard the shepherd say: “What luck!
englishEquivalent: Had my goat been seized by the neck, it would be already dead’.

translation: One kindness prepares for another.
englishEquivalent: One good turn deserves another.

translation: When lions have gone, hyenas dance.
englishEquivalent: When the cat is away, the mice will play.

translation: The woman’s trills are shouted at the mortar.
explanation: The proverb refers to the songs and shouts of the women crushing the sugar cane to be brewed; and means that such songs are sung only on that occasion.
englishEquivalent: Everything has its time.

translation: The animal that treads on the earth may find its trapper.
explanation: The proverb means: ‘To err is human’.

translation: The poor and the thorn do not sleep.
explanation: The former, say the Kikuyu, is kept awake by his anxieties whilst the latter is always on the alert in order to sting anyone who happens to touch it.
englishEquivalent: Poverty breeds strife.

translation: The poor man is robbed even of his awl.
englishEquivalent: The poor man turns his cake, and another comes and takes it away.

translation: One fly spoils an ox-hide.
englishEquivalent: A little leak will sink a great ship.

translation: The fly has no sinew.
englishEquivalent: You cannot make a silk purse from a sow’s ear.

kikuyu: Ngi irathagwo ūigana mūkiha ūria īri naguo
translation: The fly is bled proportionately to its veins.
englishEquivalent: If you squeeze a cork, you will get but little juice.

translation: The neck does not grow above the head.
englishEquivalent: Everything to its place.

kikuyu: Ngingo ya mūria-ng’ūrū ni githitū na rūrigi
translation: The neck of him who sells too dear, is all amulets and necklaces (for nobody buys from him).
englishEquivalent: All covet, all lose.

translation: Oxen are not found through laziness.
englishEquivalent: Laziness travels so slowly that poverty soon overtakes it.

translation: When the cow is left to the care of a man who is not the owner, the calves are suckled only when they cry.
englishEquivalent: Look to the cow, and the sow, and the wheat mow, and all will be well now.

translation: The heart eats what it likes.
englishEquivalent: Love is blind.

kikuyu: Ngoro ni mũrũ wa nyina na mündũ
translation: Every man's brother is his heart.
englishEquivalent: Few hearts that are not double, few tongues that are not cloves.

kikuyu: Ngoro ni mũtĩtĩ mũtumanu na ndũngitonyeka ni mündũ
translation: The heart is a thick forest which cannot be penetrated by anybody.
englishEquivalent: What is in one's heart man's eyes see not.

translation: The heart does not curse for nothing.
explanation: The proverb means that one does not repine nor swear at another without a reason.
englishEquivalent: Everything has its reason.

translation: Hearts do not meet (converge) like roads.
englishEquivalent: Eat a peck of salt with a man before you trust him.

translation: The beads one has chosen have no imperfection.
englishEquivalent: Every man thinks his own geese swans.

translation: (Even) drinking liquid fat comes to an end.
explanation: Liquid fat of animals is esteemed a dainty by the Kikuyu.
englishEquivalent: All good things come to an end.

translation: The bedbug prospers on a piece of wood.
englishEquivalent: There is a special providence in the fall of a sparrow.

translation: The beard-pincers are not inherited.
explanation: It must be remembered that the Kikuyu do not shave but pull out the beard with pincers forged by native blacksmiths . The proverb means that there are some things which are so personal that the father does not bequeath them to his son; he has to get his own.

translation: The fame is never up to its owner's merit, He that doth good for praise only, merieth but a puff of wind.
To good clothes no ornament is added.

kikuyu: Ngwa mbere ti noru ta ngwa thutha
translation: The first fall is not as bad as the second fall.
Every man's tale is good till another's be told.

kikuyu: Ngware ikirara mutti iguru ndiatigiro kuri kwega
translation: Potatoes are not praised when they are dug out (but when they are eaten).
englishEquivalent: The proof of the pudding is in the eating.

translation: The francolin is not killed in the courtyard.
explanation: The francolin is not killed in the courtyard. According to Kikuyu superstition to kill a francolin found on one's courtyard brings in misfortune. If anybody has done it, he must slaughter a goat to propitiate the spirits.
englishEquivalent: There is a measure in all things.

kikuyu: Ngware nyinyi iri na mukuririe wayo
translation: The little francolin has its way of scratching.
englishEquivalent: Every man his way.

translation: A hero dies with the other.
explanation: The proverb refers to the days of war before the advent of Europeans, when warriors went together to plunder and were bound to win or to die together.

translation: One strong man only cannot close the ford of a river.
A strong man is not overpowered by his task.
A powerful man does not dominate two seasons.
A strong man is the ornament of his age-group.
Strength does not dwell in the calves of the legs.
explanation: The proverb means that one's strength does not dwell in one's appearance, but rather in mind and virtue.

kikuyu: Njau irĩ ndoge nyina ni ndoge
translation: If the calf has been poisoned, also its mother has been (For they ordinarily eat the same food).
englishEquivalent: Like father, like son.

translation: He who waits does not arrive.
englishEquivalent: Never leave that till tomorrow which you can do today.

translation: 'Do to me and do to me' have no bitterness.
explanation: The proverb means that a person cannot complain on receiving from others the same kind of treatment as he had given to them.

translation: The road never says to the traveller, 'Take a rest'.
A short way is only the way to bed.
explanation: The proverb is told when one wants to cut short a discussion, or when one wants a whole night to reflect before making up one's mind.
englishEquivalent: Consult with your pillow.

translation: The elephant is not overpowered by its tusks.
The beer is a thing that unites (the tongue).
englishEquivalent: When the wine is in the wit is out.

translation: A bird that picks food with the beak does not collect food for another bird.
The bee has not got two stings.
explanation: The proverb is told to greedy people, who when given something are not satisfied and want more.
englishEquivalent: Much wants more.

translation: A strong man's club is tested by foreigners.
explanation: The proverb means that it is foreigners who actually test the strength of a man, for they dare measure themselves with him. Whilst the people who live with him, judging his strength as a thing beyond any doubt, are afraid of testing it.
englishEquivalent: The proof of a pudding is in the eating.

translation: Slander is worse than a river in flood.
englishEquivalent: The most dangerous of wild beasts is a slanderer, of tame ones a flatterer.

translation: Calumnies are (as plentiful as) rich people’s beads.
An old ox is not refused water.
englishEquivalent: Old age is honourable.

translation: Bad meat is tasted with the mouth.
englishEquivalent: The proof of the pudding is in the eating.

translation: Woman, remember that the mouth is sometimes covered with a branch.
englishEquivalent: A woman cannot keep a secret.

translation: One gourd (of beer) does not stop the gift.
explanation: The Kikuyu used to send their relations and friends presents of native beer in gourds. The proverb means that the breaking of one gourd in transit does not prevent the delivery of the others.

translation: A short gourd (of beer) is not given as a present.
englishEquivalent: A slight gift, small thanks.

translation: The grass of the courtyard is not eaten.
explanation: The proverb means that oxen do not eat the grass growing near their pen, for they know it has been fertilized with their droppings. But the oxen which come from another pen and have no reason for loathing such good pasture feed on it with delight. The proverb is applied to the girls who ordinarily are not loved by the young men of their village, to whom the girls of other places look handsomer.
englishEquivalent: Never a prophet was valued in his own country.

translation: To possess and to send for is not the same.
englishEquivalent: There is many a slip 'twixt the cup and the lip.

translation: Beauty does no good.
What is found quickly, is quickly lost.
englishEquivalent: Quick come, quick lost.

kikuyu: Nyoni kirimũ yakaga irigũ ikũrũ igũrũ itoi riatemwo
translation: The foolish bird nests on an old banana tree and does not know that it will be cut down.

kikuyu: Nyoni yakaga nyũmba na mũthice ūmwe
translation: The bird makes its nest only with one beak.
Death's thirst is never quenched.
englishEquivalent: There is no medicine against death.

translation: If the hut burns, its owner gets warm.
The house covers many things.
englishEquivalent: There is not always good cheer where the chimney smokes.

translation: The clan and 'rika' cannot be cancelled.
explanation: People initiated in a particular season are banded together in an age-group and are said to be of the same rika'. They are supposed to be obliged to help one another, like the members of the same clan.

translation: A granary cannot be pushed into a hut.
explanation: Don't bite off more than you can chew.
englishEquivalent: K.P.-D

translation: The little house discusses its affairs by night (because they are not worth discussion by day with waste of time).

kikuyu: Nyũmba nyinyi yoragana yathama, yoragwo yathama
translation: If a member of a small family is killed or kills another, the family moves (since it may be unable to defend itself).
The pot cooks the food and does not eat it.
englishEquivalent: Bees that make honey, do not taste it.

translation: A rotten gourd seed does not germinate.
englishEquivalent: Immoral people seldom get offspring.

translation: The pot in which fat is stored does not break (for it is well fed).
The cooking pot from which many people await their food, does not lack him who takes it from the fire.
explanation: In like way, the problem in which many people are interested, will have one able to solve it.

translation: Every man makes up his own bed.
englishEquivalent: Every bird must hatch its own eggs.

kikuyu: O mũndũ ahuragia mwaki na mwihirito wake
translation: Every man scratches in his fire and in his ‘mwihirito’.
explanation: ‘Mwihirito’ is the space between any two of the three stones of the Kikuyu hearth.
englishEquivalent: Everyone should sweep before his own door.

translation: The food which one takes as provision for one’s journey, is not carried by another person.
englishEquivalent: Take heed is a good read.

translation: The foetus which is in the womb carries the future.
explanation: The Kikuyu use this proverb to mean that only God knows the future, just as only God causes a foetus to be a male or a female.
englishEquivalent: The future is in the hands of God.

translation: The name is a useless thing.
englishEquivalent: From our ancestors came our names, but from our virtues our honours.

kikuyu: Riu ni thatũ, no riu ringĩ ni mbura ya mahiga
translation: Now we have misty weather, but after a while it hails.
englishEquivalent: To become worse and worse.

kikuyu: Rigi ria nyũmba ritirutagwo ria gũtiria nyũmba ya
translation: ũngĩ The door of one’s hut is not taken to close another’s hut.
englishEquivalent: He who has but one coat cannot lend it.

translation: One does not lose the age-grade nor the clan-right.
explanation: Kikuyu circumcised in a particular season are banded together in an age group to which a name is given, after a special event of the season. This age-grade as well as the clan imply certain rights which no Kikuyu wants to give up.
englishEquivalent: No man is willing to waive his rights.

kikuyu: Riko na mwana na nda itiũĩ ‘kwaga’
translation: The hearth, the child and the belly ignore the word ‘lack’.

kikuyu: Riko na mwana na nda itiganagia
translation: The hearth, the child and the belly never have enough.
Cross the stream where it roars.
englishEquivalent: Still waters run deep.

translation: The watering eye makes the nose water.
englishEquivalent: When the head aches all the body is the worse.

translation: The eye, which is disturbed, waters.
englishEquivalent: Let sleeping dogs lie.

translation: The eye scorns heroes; i.e.
explanation: it can judge falsely of what it sees.
englishEquivalent: Never judge from appearances.

translation: The eye discerns the beauty but not the kindness (of a person).
The eye is not a piece of cloth (which can be thrown away).
englishEquivalent: The eye is the pearl of the face.

translation: The eye is not a thing which can be asked for.
The sun does not wait for the judge.
englishEquivalent: The sun may do its duty though your grapes do not ripen.

kikuyu: Riũa ritiri gitonga no ngia theri
translation: For the sun there are no rich, but only poor people.
explanation: The proverb means that in the dry season neither the rich nor the poor people can plant.
englishEquivalent: The sun shines on the just and the unjust.

translation: A short hide is of no value.
The owner of the goat does not give away its hide.
explanation: The proverb refers to the fact that the skin of a slaughtered goat belongs by right to the animal's owner, who does not allow anybody else to have it for nothing.
englishEquivalent: Metaphorically it means that nobody gives his life but for a cause worthy of it.

translation: The string (too tightly strung) breaks the bow.
englishEquivalent: A bow long bent at last waxeth weak.

kikuyu: Rūgendo rwa njũa na rwa mbũri iĩĩtwaranaga
translation: Hides and goats do not keep the same pace (when they are taken to market).
explanation: In fact goats go on foot while hides are carried by men, who actually go more quickly.
englishEquivalent: Every man in his way.

translation: The cutting knife does not lack bruises.
englishEquivalent: Touch pitch and you will be defiled.

translation: A knife too well sharpened easily breaks.
englishEquivalent: To kill with kindness.

translation: A tree branch cannot put forth a man.
englishEquivalent: Nothing comes out of the sack but what was in it.

translation: The river is made bigger by the small springs.
englishEquivalent: Little winnings make a heavy purse.

translation: A river is not made to flow out of its bed.
englishEquivalent: Every sparrow to its ear of wheat.

translation: An occurrence in the morning can be of more importance than one of the night before.
englishEquivalent: Problems should be dealt with in order of importance, not in order of time.

translation: Take hold of your clothes where there is no hole (lest you would tear them even more).

kikuyu: Rũmwe rũranagwo rũkirĩa: rwagomania hĩa rũgacokanwo
translation: The members of one clan can leave one another, but after all they return (to help one another).
englishEquivalent: Mutual assistance is one of the pacts by which members of one clan are bound.

translation: The clan does not break, but its members can separate.
The fate, dear man, cannot be avoided.
The firewood which is in the pile laughs at the firewood which is already in the fire.
englishEquivalent: Today me, tomorrow thee.

translation: The knife which has been unsheathed does not return into its sheath without having done some work.
The poor man’s tongue is always thin.
explanation: Since a poor man’s tongue is supposed to utter only words of no importance, so it is said to be thin. The meaning of the proverb is that a poor man will never be listened to.
englishEquivalent: The poor man’s wisdom is as useless as a palace in a wilderness.

translation: If you have a pain at home, you have it in the field too.
englishEquivalent: No place is fenced against suffering.

kikuyu: Rũri na Komũ rũri na Kaigũ wa nyina
translation: If Komu has it, Kaigu, his brother, has it too.
explanation: ‘Komũ’ and ‘Kaigũ’ are used in Kikuyu proverbs to denote brothers. The proverb means that if a man has something (either good or bad) his brother has a share in it too.

translation: Family-ties cannot be washed at the river, i.e.
englishEquivalent: cannot be untied.

kikuyu: Rũrigĩ rũri nja rũtiagaga gĩa kuoha
translation: The string in the courtyard does not lack something to tie (in due time, although at present it may seem a useless thing).
The string can be useful until a rope (of hide) can be got Little is better than nothing.
The knife cuts him who shaves another.
englishEquivalent: A knave is often caught in his own trap.

translation: The ‘rũthuko’ spreads its smell from its container.
explanation: ‘Rũthuko’ is a medicine given by a witch-doctor to a trapper to help him to attract prey, or to a shepherd to call his sheep. It should be burnt and the smell of the smoke is supposed to be a call for animals. But natives believe the medicine to exercise its power even from its container. The proverb compares the smell of the medicine to the words of man, which are supposed to be a reflection of his mind and means that one can judge him from his words.

translation: One piece of wood only does not keep the fire alight.
englishEquivalent: One stroke fells not an oak.

translation: The log which I myself cut has no knot.
englishEquivalent: Every potter praises his own pot, and more if it be broken.

translation: The stream drowns even the swimmer.

kikuyu: Rũ ni rũrigi rwa kũruta rũngĩ kinya
translation: That is a thread for pulling another thread out of the ‘kinya’.
explanation: ‘Kinya’ is a calabash used to draw water or to hold gruel. Here it is taken to mean the hidden place wherein one’s secrets are kept. The proverb is told to people who ask indirect questions for discovering what they cannot learn directly.

translation: The pain is felt by its owner (and not by another).
Pain cannot be felt by one for the other.
Take out the pus with the thorn.
englishEquivalent: Do nothing by halves.

translation: One peg only does not stretch out a skin.
englishEquivalent: No living man all things can.

translation: Love means trouble.
englishEquivalent: Love is a sweet tyranny, because the lover endures his torments willingly.

translation: Love exceeds reward.
englishEquivalent: Love is not mean.

kikuyu: Rwendo rwarutire mwana wa nderi igũrũ
translation: Love put the eaglet out of its nest.
explanation: The Kikuyu say that the young eagles, if left alone in the nest by their parents try to do as the parents do out of love for them and leap out of the nest; but in so doing they kill themselves.
englishEquivalent: Love is blind.

translation: Males’ pity has no milk.
explanation: It means that men are unable to stop the crying of a baby by suckling it. Metaphorically the proverb means that men feel no less pity than women, although they show less.

translation: The owner’s beauty does not break.
englishEquivalent: Every man thinks his own geese swans.

translation: Blood has need of no friendship.
explanation: The proverb means that the best friendship is the one that comes from relationship; for, as it has been told before, all the members of a clan are tied by the bond of helping one another.
englishEquivalent: Blood is thicker than water.

translation: The ‘thatũ’ is smeared with fat and driven out.
explanation: ‘Thatũ’ is the name of a big caterpillar which infests sweet potato plantations. To the Kikuyu it is a creature of bad omen; that is why, when it happens to enter their huts they do not kill it, but rather smear it with fat and take it out carefully to propitiate the spirit.
englishEquivalent: Misfortunes that cannot be avoided, must be sweetened.

translation: Two 'thegere' are not overpowered by a beehive.
explanation: 'Thegere' is a small mammal, about the size of a pole-cat common in Kikuyu land. It is fond of honey. The proverb means that only one 'thegere' would be unable to pull a beehive down from a tree. But if two of them join together, they easily succeed in overturning and emptying it.
englishEquivalent: Union is strength.

translation: He who laughs at others will be laughed at.
The earth and the sky do not know each other.
explanation: The proverb means that nobody can foretell the weather.

kikuyu: Thiga ni mũuu: marara nja gũtiri
translation: 'Thiga' is circumcised: there is no reward for passing the night in the courtyard.
explanation: 'Thiga' means a certain fellow. The proverb originates in one of the many customs relating to the Kikuyu ceremony of circumcision. On the eve of the circumcision-day women and girls gather at the hut of the candidate and sing for a great part in the night; not gratuitously, but in the hope of getting food and beer from the candidate's mother. But if when the rite is completed, she makes as an excuse that now the child is circumcised and refuses to give them what they expect, they start singing the above strain, meaning: 'Have no recourse to the idle pretext that your son is now circumcised; but rather give us the reward to which we are entitled after a night's singing and dancing'.
englishEquivalent: Eaten bread is soon forgotten.

translation: The 'thina' has no roots.
explanation: 'Thina' is the name of a kind of leafless plant growing on trees. It also means affliction, troubles, sadness, poverty.
englishEquivalent: Troubles pass.

translation: Affliction does not leave a place which is already known to her.
englishEquivalent: One danger is seldom overcome without another.

translation: Affliction does not last.
englishEquivalent: After a storm comes a calm.

kikuyu: Thina ni rūhiũ rwa gūicūhia mūro
translation: Affliction is a good knife to sharpen the ‘mūro’.
explanation: ‘Mūro’ is a short stick used to beat the earth, to plant, to dig out potatoes, etc.
englishEquivalent: Necessity sharpens industry.

translation: The duiker cannot help panting.
englishEquivalent: The leopard cannot change his spots.

translation: The duiker is not found without head stripes.
englishEquivalent: Man is what God has made him and nothing else.

translation: Quiver means bow (for there is no quiver but it has also its bow).
A quiver upside down cannot fail to pour out its arrows.
explanation: The proverb is an excuse for an error which depends only on human weakness.
englishEquivalent: To err is human.

translation: The ‘thiari’ does not hover above a poor man’s house.
explanation: ‘Thiari’ is the tick-bird. The proverb says that this bird does not stay with the poor for there are no oxen to provide ticks.
englishEquivalent: A poor man has no friends.

translation: The debt of poisoning a person is a debt which cannot be paid.
explanation: All the other crimes can be paid for with a number of goats, but the crime of bewitching must be expiated by heavier punishment.

translation: Friendships dissolve.

kikuyu: Thiriti ni ya andū erī, ya atatū ni rūmena
translation: Friendship can exist between two people, friendship of three people would mean strife.
englishEquivalent: Two’s company, three’s none.

translation: Friendship finishes if there are whisperings.
Buying (and selling) brings in much noise but no strife.
Buying and selling has neither mother nor son.
englishEquivalent: Friendship is friendship and business is business.

kikuyu: Thome wa anake ndūri thogora no tharo
translation: Young unmarried men do not buy in their ‘thome’: they steal things.
explanation: ‘Thome’ is the pathway leading up to the entrance of the Kikuyu homestead. It is made in the shape of a narrow passage which can be closed at night or in time of danger. The proverb means that nothing orderly can be done when only youngsters are present.

translation: Shyness has no sucking.
explanation: It means that if a calf is shy it will be afraid to approach its mother and consequently will get no milk.

translation: Too much shyness means miserliness.
englishEquivalent: There is measure in all things.

translation: The enemy does not fall where one throws him.
englishEquivalent: Man proposes, God disposes.

translation: An enemy does not lack someone to shave him; i.e.
englishEquivalent: to keep him informed of what is going about him, and very often to give him help.

kikuyu: Thumbi iri nyone, mwene ni muone
translation: If one sees the ostrich-feather head-dress, one sees also the owner of it.
explanation: The Kikuyu warriors used to pass over the head and under the chin a strap carrying ostrich feathers. Such a head-dress is used today only by young men at the circumcision ceremonies. The proverb means that if you see anyone wearing such an ornament, you easily recognize him as a warrior.

translation: Choose between dying and living; i.e.
englishEquivalent: between death and life, war and peace.

translation: It is proper of the ram to have a good tail.
explanation: It means that the good side of many a thing is not found at the beginning of it, but at the end, just as the best part of the ram is not its head, but its fat tail.
englishEquivalent: The best fish swim near the bottom.

translation: The afterwards is wide.
Where men have passed there is not a single feather to pick up.

kikuyu: Thutha wa maündu mothe ni Mwathani
translation: After all, there is God.
englishEquivalent: Man proposes, God disposes.

kikuyu: Tiga gũkunga hira-ini na tama mwerũ
translation: If you wear white clothes do not hide in a place where the grass has been burnt (for you would easily be discovered).
explanation: The proverb means that it is useless to tell lies that are obviously lies.

translation: Do not show wisdom where there is wisdom.
englishEquivalent: To carry coals to Newcastle.

translation: Cease repining: go on; you are not like a child that licks the ‘kĩihũri’.
explanation: Kĩihũri’ is a half calabash used as a ladle or an eating bowl. The proverb means that a man must not be timid like a child that is afraid of his mother’s rebuke and dares not lay down the ‘kĩihũri’ used for gruel, if it is not licked.
englishEquivalent: Fortune helps them that help themselves.

translation: Do not expect blood from a fly.
englishEquivalent: If you squeeze a cork, you will get but little juice.

kikuyu: Tiga kwaria na kanua ka ngoma
translation: Stop talking with the mouth of the ‘ngoma’.
explanation: ‘Ngoma’ are the spirits of the departed in which the Kikuyu firmly believe.
englishEquivalent: Keep your tongue within your teeth.

translation: Stop teaching the leopard how to climb a tree.
englishEquivalent: Don’t teach your grandmother how to knit.

translation: We do not give twice to the hyena.
englishEquivalent: Once bitten, twice shy.

translation: The man who has a family does not adorn his arm with finery.
englishEquivalent: Children are certain cares, but uncertain comforts.

translation: A sip is better than a feast.
explanation: The proverb means that a sip of beer given to him who happens to call on a friend during a beer drinking is more appreciated than a feast to which one has been invited (and has therefore waited for).

translation: Many hands eating (from the same dish) hate one another.
explanation: Two cats and a mouse, two wives in one house, two dogs and a bone never agree in one.

translation: He who is in need sends his boy when there is still the dew.
englishEquivalent: Need makes the naked man trot.

translation: The person who is in need does not feel ashamed.
englishEquivalent: Need makes the naked queen spin.

translation: It is the person who feels the need (of sleeping) that prepares the bed.
englishEquivalent: Let him that is cold blow the coal.

translation: (Even) bravery does not cross two valleys (at one time).
englishEquivalent: Samson was a strong man, yet could not pay money before he had it.

translation: To return (to the same thing, argument, etc.) is foolishness.
englishEquivalent: A tale twice told is cabbage twice sold.

translation: You are slandered without being thrown away.
(The time will come when) you will step on the ‘mūhā’ in a place where there is no other plant.
explanation: ‘Mūhā’ is a common forest tree yielding a very poor timber. The proverb means that he who despises this tree because it is of little value and there is plenty of good timber, will go so far as to scorn it even when no better timber is available.
englishEquivalent: Half a loaf is better than no bread.

kikuyu: Ũgakinya na mūtwe, wirite nī magūrū
translation: You will move on the head thinking it is the feet.
explanation: It is said to proud people who think they know everything .
englishEquivalent: Do as most men do and men will speak well of thee.

translation: You shall have pains like the eye that opens in the morning.
explanation: The proverb is a curse, and refers to the pain which one’s eyes are supposed to feel when, after a night’s pleasant dreams, they open again to this world’s miseries.

translation: Too great a wisdom breaks the axe.
englishEquivalent: Too much breaks the bag.

translation: Wisdom does not go in front as foolishness; i.e.
explanation: is not so easily attained as foolishness.
englishEquivalent: No man is born wise or learned.

translation: Knowledge is power.
(There is) wisdom (that is) a bluff.
englishEquivalent: All is not gold that glitters.

translation: Wisdom outweighs strength.

kikuyu: Ūgĩ wa arũme ūtemaga ta hiũ
translation: Men's skill cuts like knives.
englishEquivalent: Words are for women, actions for men.

translation: Only one man's ability cannot till (all the fields).
englishEquivalent: No living man all things can.

translation: He who has been invited to eat meat does not waste time looking for good clothes.
explanation: The proverb means that if anyone has received an invitation for a feast he does not waste time in adorning himself at the risk of arriving too late.

kikuyu: Ugithondekera mūciĩ ndũngĩuga ni ūrikora ūngĩ
translation: While you adorn your house, you do not imagine that you will find another (more adorned than yours).
explanation: The proverb refers to self confident people who go to discuss a question with the certainty of getting the best of it, and do not think that perhaps they will meet an adversary stronger than they are.
englishEquivalent: The first caper of fools is to esteem themselves wise.

translation: You smear yourself with misfortune.
explanation: The proverb is told as an advice to people who are on the point of doing something which sooner or later will become a cause of misfortune.
englishEquivalent: He that cuts himself wilfully, will deserve no balsam.

translation: Scabies is contracted (by contact).
englishEquivalent: A rotten sheep infects the whole flock.

kikuyu: Ūhiĩ ni umagwo, no ūka ndumagwo
translation: The man comes out of childhood, but the woman never comes out of womanhood.
englishEquivalent: To understand the proverb, it must be remembered that 109

translation: Asking for something is like turning (potatoes in the fire or meat on the spit).
explanation: The proverb means that he who wants to succeed in a petition tries all ways, just as he who is roasting his food turns it on all sides.

kikuyu: Úhoro wa maitho ti wa ñuthiñi
translation: What one sees with one's eyes is not what one hears from another's tongue.
englishEquivalent: One eye-witness is better than ten hearsays.

translation: He who is sated has no affection.
englishEquivalent: What cannot be cured must be endured.

translation: Oh, for the (good) past!
explanation: This is an expression often heard in the mouths of Kikuyu elders and corresponds to: 'Past and to come seem best: things present, worst'.

translation: The Masai have had their fill of flour.
explanation: The Kikuyu used to sell maize and millet flour to their neighbours the Masai. But if they happened to sell it a little too dear, the flour trade became the spark which kindled one of the many raids which ended only when the British Government confined the Masai to their present territory. The proverb had the meaning of an alarm, as to say:

translation: Joy does not last.
englishEquivalent: Pleasant hours fly fast.

kikuyu: Ũkũndihia ũgacoka kũnjuria ndario ni kũ?
translation: You wound me and then ask what is ailing me?
Old age does not shout any notice-cry.
englishEquivalent: Time is the rider that breaks youth.

translation: Old age is like being lame.
explanation: The proverb is told by or to old women.
englishEquivalent: Old bees yield no honey.

translation: Old age eats youth.
englishEquivalent: Old age creeps in.

translation: You want the salt before the person who burned the salt-grass.
explanation: To understand this proverb it must be borne in mind that, before the arrival of Europeans, the Kikuyu obtained salt from the ashes of salt-grass. (See also No.
englishEquivalent: 629.) No cross, no crown.

translation: Home affairs are known by him who sleeps in the home, not by him who only comes in the morning.
englishEquivalent: None knows the weight of another's burden.

translation: You sometimes eat me by cunningness.
englishEquivalent: In this proverb 'to eat' means 'to cheat'.

kikuyu: Ūndū ūkwendwo ndūtanukagwo ni kūmerio ūmeragio
translation: The thing that one finds palatable is not chewed, but it is swallowed quickly.
If you hear a goat moan, it is because she has been bitten.
englishEquivalent: No smoke without fire.

translation: One must not return on the work done.
explanation: The proverb means that one must not be too attentive to the details of his work if one wants to finish it, since— Perfection is not of this world.

translation: If you go too carefully, (the chance) will pass away.
englishEquivalent: Sleeping foxes catch no poultry.

kikuyu: Ūngīguā kaana gakiuga ūndū ūgakahūra: menya
translation: kaiguīte na ithe When you hear your child say anything, you beat him; remember that he says what he has heard from his father.
englishEquivalent: Children pick up words as pigeons peas, and utter them again as God shall please.

kikuyu: Ūngīria irio cia mūthembā ūmwe iri kinyiria
translation: If you eat ever of the same food, it becomes bitter: it is a good thing to change.
englishEquivalent: Change of pasture makes fat calves.

translation: If you see a quiet snake, it is because it swallowed another snake.
englishEquivalent: Beware of a silent dog and still water.

translation: He who has tasted (food) has its appetite.
explanation: The proverb means that, if a man has willingly started to do some job, he is not satisfied until he completes it.

translation: He who is in trouble lacks (also) a field for his son.
englishEquivalent: Misfortunes seldom come alone.

kikuyu: Ūri kūhitia na mbugi, ndūrathaga na njoya
translation: If you have missed with the point (of the arrow) you do not hit with the feathers.
englishEquivalent: Resist the beginnings.

kikuyu: Ūri kūngariūra ta mūtura wa ihī
translation: You have tried to roast me as boys roast goat’s bowels.
explanation: When a goat or an ox is slaughtered, it is a Kikuyu custom to give the bowels to the uncircumcised for them to roast. The proverb is a contemptuous expression meaning ‘I know that you want to deceive me: but don’t expect to succeed as easily as boys succeed in roasting the bowels they are given’.

translation: If you despair you are not cured.
explanation: The proverb refers to women who go to the witch-doctors for a remedy for their sterility.
englishEquivalent: Not to have hope is the poorest of all conditions.

translation: If you are good you are known.
englishEquivalent: Good wine needs no bush.

kikuyu: Ūri na ithe ndaringagwo wa ngoro
translation: He who has a father is not knocked down by any of those words or deeds that hurt one’s heart (for he has somebody to defend him).
He who has many friends is not caught by darkness in the road; i.e.
englishEquivalent: he has a lodging for the night.

translation: You are a person who neither leaves nor waits for me.
englishEquivalent: To have two strings to one bow.

translation: Have you ever seen an unsheathed knife (a thing that has frightened you)?
englishEquivalent: Scalded cats fear even cold water.

translation: The tilling does not come to an end.
Misfortune that has put down roots, does not finish.

kikuyu: Uri ndiri indo, ni heho iri indo
translation: It is not warning oneself (staying at home) that makes one rich, but talking with many people.
englishEquivalent: God helps them who help themselves.

translation: Two persons, who have both cooked their food, do not beg from one another.
The work is done if one does it.
englishEquivalent: If you want anything done, do it yourself.

translation: Also for the man who has not yet received a present, there is something put aside for him.
englishEquivalent: Everything comes to him who waits.

translation: He whose seeds have not germinated, does not lay down his 'kigina'.
explanation: 'Kigina' means the seeds put by for planting next season.
englishEquivalent: Perseverance kills the game.

translation: Prodigality ruined the man who used to give away his oven.
explanation: The legend, from which this proverb originates, tells that a very rich man used to present all his visitors with

translation: A poor man's generosity is lost in his heart (for he has nothing to show it with).
The person who has not a small bag, has a small basket.
englishEquivalent: Every man has his lot.

translation: He who has nothing has no heart.
explanation: The proverb means that a poor man, though refused what he asks for, does not feel so much pain as a rich man would, for the latter knows the difference between possessing and not possessing what one needs.
englishEquivalent: Nothing have, nothing crave.

translation: A blind man does not sew a gourd.
explanation: The Kikuyu make use of the dried shell of gourds as dippers and ladles. They mend them with a rough thread when they crack.
englishEquivalent: Blind men should not judge of colours.

translation: A poor man is not invited to a private discussion.
He is a person that does not eat other's food, nor his own.
explanation: The proverb refers to people who are not able to take advantage of their own things, nor of those of other people.

translation: He who does not leave, will not find.
englishEquivalent: No gains without pains.

translation: Slipping has no hero, i.e.
explanation: nobody however clever he may be, is guaranteed against a fall when walking on a slippery road.
englishEquivalent: No fence against ill fortune.

translation: Nobody can avoid the slippery place that is in the courtyard.
englishEquivalent: What cannot be cured must be endured.

kikuyu: Ūthayo na ng'aragu ni mündũ na mürü wa nyina
translation: Laziness and starvation are like a man and his brother.
englishEquivalent: Laziness travels so slowly that poverty soon overtakes him.

translation: Beauty is not eaten.
englishEquivalent: Beauty will buy no beef.

translation: A rich man's old age has no bad smell.
englishEquivalent: Rich men have no faults.

kikuyu: Ūthuuri wa kanua ūkirite wa miaka
translation: Mouth's old age is better than year's old age.
explanation: The proverb means that it is of no use to be old in years, if one does not show this old age by wise words, too.
englishEquivalent: An old goat is never the more revered for his beard.

translation: Hatred does not affect all.
explanation: The proverb means that he who is hated by some people is not necessarily hated also by all the others.

translation: The picking up of only the good things does not fill one's barn.
He who does not know how to dance the 'karirui' knows how to dance the 'waci'.
He who does not know one thing, knows another.
englishEquivalent: Every man hath his lot.

translation: Riches are not attained by running.
Riches are a shadow.
englishEquivalent: Riches have wings.

translation: Riches have no bird of ill omen.

kikuyu: Ūtonga wa mūici ndūthunaga, na ni ūteaga wake
translation: Unlawful riches do not increase, but rather spoil the lawful ones.
englishEquivalent: Ill-gotten things seldom prosper.

translation: One does not sew clothes by night.
englishEquivalent: There is a time for all things.

kikuyu: Wa githi ndagiragia wa kio akagia
translation: He who feels envy cannot prevent a man of energy from becoming enriched.
englishEquivalent: Envy never enriched any man.

translation: The fire which comes from afar dies out in the way.
englishEquivalent: Out of sight, out of mind.

kikuyu: Wa hwalini warugwo ni wa kiroko
translation: What happens in the morning, surpasses what happened the preceding evening.
englishEquivalent: Every day brings a new light.

translation: The fool's staff (walking stick) is used by the wise.
explanation: The proverb means that something belonging to a fool may help the wise, as the fool does not know how to use it to his benefit.

translation: The goat bone is not thrown away if it is not completely chipped.
He who sees does not err.
englishEquivalent: One eye-witness is better than ten hearsays.

translation: Yaws causes one to be attacked by chicken pox too.
englishEquivalent: Misfortunes seldom come alone.

translation: God's fire keeps alight with 'magoto'.
explanation: 'Magoto' is dry banana bark which is much used for thatching but of no use as firewood. The proverb means that God can kindle a fire and keep it alive with unsuitable materials.
englishEquivalent: With God all things are possible.

translation: The work of many people scorns him who does not do it.
explanation: Work, however heavy it may be, if done by many people seems to become light for each worker. This is why the proverb says that he who refused to do his part should be despised by the work itself.

translation: The squirrel walks in the dew.
explanation: The proverb originates in the fact that the squirrel is often seen in the road by early travellers, which would suggest that it rises very early in the morning. The Kikuyu say the proverb as a reply when, met by friends in the road, they are asked about the place they are coming from and why they are travelling so early. It means: I start my work early because I am like the squirrel that knows that morning hours are the best.
englishEquivalent: The early bird catches the worm.

translation: A wicked man's arrow emits its unpleasant smell even if hidden in the quiver.
englishEquivalent: Stinking fish are felt from afar.

translation: The fire of the 'Mwangi' does not smoke twice.
explanation: 'Mwangi' is the name of one of the major ruling generations . The representatives of each generation stand in authority and are responsible for the conduct of public affairs all over Kikuyu land for about thirty years. After such a term there is a ceremony of handing over the custody of the affairs of the tribe from one generation to the next. The handing-over rite takes months and even years to complete. When the Consolata Fathers entered Kikuyu land in 1902 the Maina generation was handing over its powers to the Mwangi generation, which in its turn has already begun to hand over to the Irungu.
englishEquivalent: Time flies away without delay.

translation: The case of the good man is like the bad one's.
explanation: The sentence is said by elders when judging tribal questions, and means that all people have the same right and nobody can expect to have his case discussed before another's: every one must wait his turn.

translation: One hates to see the blood of a thing that belongs to him.
explanation: The proverb means that one’s heart is affected by the pains of the persons and animals whom one loves.
englishEquivalent: Whom we love best, them we want to be happy.

translation: What is inside the body is not known.
englishEquivalent: No one knows the weight of another’s burden.

translation: The work one imposed on oneself is never impossible.
englishEquivalent: Where there is a will there is a way.

translation: He who used to dance, now looks on.
He who has ever been black will never become white.
englishEquivalent: A leopard cannot change his spots.

translation: He who drinks (beer in company) drinks an arrow at the same time.
explanation: The proverb means that people who drink beer together as a token of friendship, drink as well an arrow which they will use to shoot one another as soon as their friendship breaks.

translation: He who has eaten (all his food) vexes him who has put some aside.
englishEquivalent: A fool and his money are soon parted.

translation: He who used to jump across now wades through.
englishEquivalent: Old age creeps in.

translation: You are one who eats the fruit of what your father has planted.
You are only thirsty when somebody has drawn the water.
explanation: The proverb is told to lazy people.

translation: Good and good never meet.
englishEquivalent: Perfection is not of this world.

translation: The good is to be found beyond the bush, i.e.
explanation: the obstacle.
englishEquivalent: No gains without pains.

translation: Prosperity is found in one’s home.
englishEquivalent: Look to the cow, and the sow, and the wheat mow, and all will be well now.

translation: Illicit love spoilt the uncircumcised girl.
explanation: Sexual relation between an uncircumcised girl and a circumcised young man is considered unmentionable depravity by the Kikuyu.
englishEquivalent: The reward of unlawful pleasure is lawful pain.

translation: The open country where markets are held does not lack rubbish.
The open place where men used to stay cannot help stinking (because of the many quarrels and thefts which occur therein).
He who put something aside will not starve.
englishEquivalent: Thrift is good revenue.

translation: Many people's work kills the fool (because he does alone what should be done by many),
He who has been warned does not dispute.
englishEquivalent: A word is enough to the wise.

translation: Help yourself so that I may help you.
englishEquivalent: God helps those who help themselves.

kikuyu: Wona ciene waruta ndũngũrũ, wona ciaku wacokia
translation: ndũngũrũ When you see another's things your mouth waters; when you see your own you swallow such water.
He who had things, may stand in need.
englishEquivalent: Today gold, tomorrow dust.

translation: To have means mischief, to lack means thought.
englishEquivalent: Misfortunes tell us what fortune is.

translation: The ox one has chosen has no imperfection.
The meat one has chosen has no bone.

kikuyu: Ya kũhĩa ithiaga na ma mbere
translation: The food which cooks well is cooked with the first water.
explanation: The Kikuyu believe that the food which is not cooked in the first water would not be cooked even if new water should be added, and it is therefore to be thrown away.
englishEquivalent: Never leave that till tomorrow which you can do today.

translation: The hut thatched only with bad grass sets fire to the one covered with good thatching grass.
englishEquivalent: A rotten sheep infects the whole flock.

translation: One’s own ox has no cast in the eye.
explanation: (See also No. 992 and No.
englishEquivalent: 993.) Every man thinks his own geese swans.

translation: The goat which is of another age group eats scattering the fodder.
explanation: The proverb originates in the fact of the distinction which is kept among people of different age-grade, and means that if a member of an age group is admitted to eat food with people of another, he grows proud and shows no respect towards them.
englishEquivalent: Familiarity breeds contempt.

translation: People of the same age group slaughter the beast to be eaten even by night time.
explanation: The proverb refers to a Kikuyu custom. Young men of the same age group used to go round from village to village until they found a rich man who gave an ox or a goat for them to eat. And when the animal was found, they killed and broiled it even if the night had already come. The proverb means that one must finish what one has begun.
englishEquivalent: Do nothing by halves.

translation: The she-goat that gives birth to six kids feeds them too.
The goat that is pushed forward pushes forward the other.
englishEquivalent: One fool makes many.
